> This is similar to #8427. new Worker(new URL('./foo.js', import.meta.url)) is not supported by the dep optimizer.

> A workaround is to set optimizeDeps.exclude: ['three-gpu-pathtracer'].

Maybe a package should be able to declare to vite that it should be excluded from `optimizeDeps` in its *package.json*? So everything that depends on a given package, `three-gpu-pathtracer` in this case, does not need to make an entry in `optimizeDeps.exclude`?

> Maybe a package should be able to declare to vite that it should be excluded from optimizeDeps in its package.json?

Even better, vite analyzes dependencies for `new Worker(new URL('./*.worker.js', import.meta.url))`, and does not try to optimized the dependency. If / when the functionality is available, the optimization can be re-enabled.

Sometimes runtime errors occur after most of the page is loaded normally and the page can be used normally. In this case, will the page be replaced with the browser error overlay?

In React they prevent partial page from being rendered if there is an error, so error overlay is appropriate in all cases. It would be a nice enhancement particularly for new users and is present in CRA, NX, Snowpack etc.

@FranzSkuffka Almost but the overlay needs the frame to be defined on the error to get correct formatting. 

The code you posted will essentially show
```javascript
Error: boom
    at http://localhost:3000/src/index.tsx:17:7
```
vs what I think most people expect

```javascript
Runtime error at [filepath]
[error message]
/[filepath]:17:0
17 |      throw new Error('boom')
18 |      ^  

at [stacktrace]
```


On an unrelated note small bug in the code you posted, I think you meant to pass in the error not the event.

```javascript
window.addEventListener('error', ({error}) => showErrorOverlay(error));
```

Is `-11` column legitimate as it's pointing to where wrapper's intro `async` starts given `columnOffset`?
(So, Node's generating stack `-11` is a reasonable behavior and not a bug?)

In Vitest's use case it's kind of an edge case. We use the `async () => {}` wrapper in `node:vm` to able to use `await`, and adjust user's code with `columnOffset` for proper stack trace positions. The `async_hooks` detect the anonymous async wrapper as promise and cause negative columns.

From Node's perspective this could be a bug too. I'll file a issue there too just to be sure.
Oh well, reading through https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/43207 it seems that negative line/column in stack traces are intended feature.

I found this issue because I was trying to understand a regression I found that's blocking me updating from Vite 4.5.0 to Vite 5.2.11. I have a WASM library I built as an ES module with Emscripten, so I have `manifold.js` and `manifold.wasm` in my `built` directory. In a worker I call it like `import Module from './built/manifold';`

In Vite 4 this was working just fine both in the browser and in my node-based testing with `npm test` (what I believe you're referring to as SSR). In Vite 5, everything in the browser still works just fine, but `npm test` gives:

```
stderr | worker.test.js > Examples > Rounded Frame
TypeError: Invalid URL
    at new URL (node:internal/url:787:36)
    at Module.default (/Users/elalish/Code/manifold/bindings/wasm/examples/built/manifold.js:8:20330)
    at /Users/elalish/Code/manifold/bindings/wasm/examples/worker.ts:17:16
    at InlineWorkerRunner.runModule (file:///Users/elalish/Code/manifold/bindings/wasm/examples/node_modules/vite-node/dist/client.mjs:362:5)
    at InlineWorkerRunner.directRequest (file:///Users/elalish/Code/manifold/bindings/wasm/examples/node_modules/vite-node/dist/client.mjs:346:5)
    at InlineWorkerRunner.cachedRequest (file:///Users/elalish/Code/manifold/bindings/wasm/examples/node_modules/vite-node/dist/client.mjs:189:14)
    at InlineWorkerRunner.executeFile (file:///Users/elalish/Code/manifold/bindings/wasm/examples/node_modules/vite-node/dist/client.mjs:161:12) {
  code: 'ERR_INVALID_URL',
  input: '/built/manifold.wasm'
}
```

So even though `manifold.js` is calling `manifold.wasm` in its own directory, it can't seem to resolve the URL. But this used to work, which makes me wonder if it's actually related to this issue after all. I don't see anything obviously related in the Vite 5 migration guide. Any thoughts?

Also, the Vite docs seem to say a lot about needing plugins for loading WASM, but I'm not using any plugins with Vite 4. Has functionality been removed from core?

I am very new to this and i may be wrong, but I think that the execution order is decided by the import graph and not by position html, and since neither script imports the other they both run independently / separately. Module scripts must use imports to control execution order. DOM order does not count.

Here’s the spec (with comments about the case in this issue in italics):

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#prepare-the-script-element

> To prepare the script element given a script element el:
>
> ...
>
> 35. If el's type is "classic" and el has a src attribute, or el's type is "module": _(type is "module")_
>
>     1. Assert: el's result is "uninitialized". _(it is)_
>
>     2. If el has an async attribute or el's force async is true: _(not async, not force async – read the rest of the spec about that)_
>
>        ...
>
>     3. Otherwise, if el is not parser-inserted: _(it IS parser-inserted)_
>
>        ...
>
>     4. Otherwise, if el has a defer attribute or el's type is "module": _(type is "module")_
>
>         1. [Append](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list-append) el to its parser document's [list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#list-of-scripts-that-will-execute-when-the-document-has-finished-parsing).
>
>         2. Set el's steps to run when the result is ready to the following: set el's ready to be parser-executed to true. (The parser will handle executing the script.)

https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list-append

> To append to a [list](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list) that is not an ordered set is to add the given item to the end of the list.

https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list

> A list is a specification type consisting of a finite **ordered sequence** of items.

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#list-of-scripts-that-will-execute-when-the-document-has-finished-parsing

> Each Document has a [list](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list) of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing, which is a list of script elements, initially empty.

As far as I can tell:

- The browser keeps an **ordered list** of scripts to execute.
- The browser **appends** (adds to the end) of the list when it parses `<script type="module">`.

It makes sense that the execution order is defined. A big role of the HTML specification is to define how a document is supposed to work, so that implementations don’t have to disagree.

I shall try to explain the gigaloop:
1) Nuxt changed hash on every build, irrespective of a change in the code, for all files. Means that caching is bad and almost unusable for PWA. My application is a PWA.

7) On roll up there is some faded mention of a manualChunks feature. I tried and it works!
8) My new built system has been able to split the vendors to a separate file and the entry.js is small enough. Hashes are not changing after multiple tries... but before I could declare the win.
9) The build BREAKS!

In addition to the recommended functionality of `vite-tsconfig-paths`, which only works for the project being built, it would also be ideal to have `paths` aliases accessible within the execution of `vite.config.ts` itself.

tldr; a lot of people use `NODE_ENV` when they shouldn't. It's a common (anti)pattern. The updated docs in https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/14978 do a good job of clarifying the relationship between `NODE_ENV` and `mode`. 

...it's probably not the responsibility of the framework to tell us why it doesn't do something it shouldn't be doing. They also don't use `var` for every variable, but they don't tell us why they don't. If `mode` and/or `NODE_ENV` is something you need, be sure you know why you need it?

---

Vite controls `mode`. It does not control `NODE_ENV`. `NODE_ENV` is not vite-specific - it is an old paradigm, I think started by expressjs. It is also not official, but is so common that [npm optionally reads it](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-install) to decide whether to install `devDependencies`. pnpm fairly recently [stopped reading it](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/8827) (compare [v9](https://pnpm.io/9.x/cli/install#--prod--p) to [v10](https://pnpm.io/cli/install#--prod--p) install docs). Officially, node [calls it an antipattern](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/nodejs-the-difference-between-development-and-production).

`NODE_ENV` - vite reads this and interprets it to set `.DEV/.PROD` _at build time_. But it doesn't its own change behaviour based on that value, and doesn't overwrite `NODE_ENV` automagically (it respects all existing `process.env` values). Other libraries, or even hosting services, may depend on it, so you can't just get rid of it. Any script or command could change NODE_ENV at or before build or load time - there is a chance it could be set to something unexpected.

`mode` - vite is (obviously) not your application - it's a dev server and build tool, so it properly needs to differentiate environments, even if you agree about `NODE_ENV` being an antipattern. But you should still be cautious about how you use it IMHO. `mode` causes vite to load different environment variable files, is available only inside your app, and gets interpreted at build-time. It is the explicitly set mode of your app, and not necessarily the environment in which it's running. 

`mode` is part of `import.meta.env`, which is interpreted at build-time and values cannot be modified externally once built. `NODE_ENV` is part of `process.env` (by convention), and _can_ be modified at load time (this is probably why it's considered an antipattern to us inside your app - the same build could behave unexpectedly differently in different environments).

Some examples: you could create a vite build in dev, staging, or production mode (`vite build --mode <development/staging/production>`), all in a production environment (`NODE_ENV=production`). The example of changing the title is a good one - you might want your app to literally say the word "staging" in the title so that it's clear to QA that they are in the right place, but your build will be in a live, production-like environment (e.g. deployed to heroku or vercel or something). 

The `.env` files are a good example too. You might want different API end-points for different app modes (since vite loads different `.env` files based on mode, if they are available), but still deploy in production-like environment. Or, you might want to temporarily test your production end-points in the dev server. You can set vite's `mode` to production, even though your NODE_ENV might be development.
Afterthought - if people agree with me but still think that clarifying this is the responsibility of vite, I'd be game to work on adding some extra context to the docs.

I dug into this issue today. The reason why we had forced `keepNames: false` is due to https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/9164. If we reverted that, everyone's bundle size is likely to explode because treeshaking won't be working effectively (if they set `keepNames: true`).

I investigated the source of that issue and filed a feature request to esbuild that should fix it instead: https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/issues/3965. If that's resolved, we should be safe to revert the option.

(Note that if those are resolved, the source issue repro will generate a JS bundle rather than 0 JS, but it's less impactful in practice because treeshaking is still effective, just that it's not smart enough to reduce to 0 JS.)
But why do we need it during dev? 🤔
I guess we could allow it during dev, but build wouldn't be able to match it if we still set `keepNames: false` in build and would cause inconsistencies.

> I guess we could allow it during dev, but build wouldn't be able to match it if we still set `keepNames: false` in build and would cause inconsistencies.

True, dev won’t catch the error and it will be hard to debug when it fails in production 😔

to add to this: there a lot of scenario that requires class names to be maintained (like if you are using decorators that tracks the name of the class), that gets 'mysteriously' broken by this behaviour.

forcing `keepNames: false` behind the scene is not transparent (users might find this only in prod when they minify the code) and the fact that it cannot be overridden leaves the user no choice but to use another minifier (terser).

I appreciate your concern about bundle size but to address that you are sacrificing build correctness and that does not sound right

> I guess we could allow it during dev, but build wouldn't be able to match it if we still set `keepNames: false` in build and would cause inconsistencies.

so don't enable it by default - presumably, people who enable this will know why they did that.

and if this is enabled in a production build, issue a warning/notice explaining why the build may be larger.

> to add to this: there a lot of scenario that requires class names to be maintained (like if you are using decorators that tracks the name of the class), that gets 'mysteriously' broken by this behaviour.

yes. 😌

in fact, the [esbuild docs](https://esbuild.github.io/api/#keep-names) pretty much tell all:

> minification renames symbols to reduce code size and **bundling sometimes need to rename symbols to avoid collisions**. That changes value of the name property for many of these cases. This is usually fine because the name property is normally only used for debugging. However, **some frameworks rely on the name property for registration and binding purposes.**

so the problem doesn't solely exist because of minification - bundling itself may require renaming, which can break things.

esbuild provides this feature, with whatever caveats it may have, for well documented reasons.

I see some people are encountering this with `vite dev`. In that case, you should (1) connect the Chrome inspector to your Vite process and (2) pause the step debugger (do this shortly after starting the dev server and without loading anything in your browser). It's possible that you have a relatively complex circular directory symlink chain, and `readdirp` is being tricked into infinitely crawling those directories (but asynchronously, thereby avoiding a stack overflow). If the step debugger opens a `readdirp` file, you can be sure this is your issue. This is common if you're developing a chain of packages locally and linking one of them into your Vite project.

Using the `server.watch.ignored` option in Vite config, you can prevent `chokidar` (the file watcher that Vite uses) from watching the circular directory chain.

> [@jamesopstad](https://github.com/jamesopstad) thanks for the work on this workaround! Are there any drawbacks of using this approach since you're bypassing a fix that was made for something else?

The drawback is that it's possible to end up with multiple references for the same module. We try to discover the user's dependencies up front but in some cases dependencies are missed by Vite's dependency scanner. The scenario where this is problematic is if a new dependency is discovered late, during request handling. This may affect the pre-bundling of existing dependencies that have already been loaded and executed. In most cases this shouldn't cause issues but it's possible, for example, that there is some state stored in the module scope that leads to a mismatch.

For the time being, I think this is the right tradeoff as the `Error: There is a new version of the pre-bundle for ...` error is very frustrating and there's not currently a straightforward alternative to resolve it. It's also worth noting that the drawback outlined above was already present in Vite versions prior to 7.1.3 so we are effectively restoring that behaviour. The longer term fix is to use full-bundle mode rather than `optimizeDeps` in the Cloudflare plugin once that is supported in Vite for server environments.

The new Vite option is applied by default in v1.20.0 of `@cloudflare/vite-plugin` so if you upgrade `@cloudflare/vite-plugin`, `wrangler` and `vite` to the latest versions the issue should be resolved.

We maintain [vivliostyle-cli](https://github.com/vivliostyle/vivliostyle-cli), a Node.js CLI application that loads JavaScript configuration files. We are currently working on adding TypeScript configuration file support (`.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`) using Node.js 22+ `--experimental-strip-types` flag (similar to how Prettier works).

The issue arises in [our test environment](https://github.com/vivliostyle/vivliostyle-cli/blob/40b4cdecfd409207bd6e4271d839296e681eea69/tests/config-typescript.test.ts#L57-L67). We use Vitest to test the config loading functionality, and when Vitest (running in SSR mode) tries to dynamically import a `.cts` file, Vite doesn't transpile it.

So to clarify: we're not using `.cts` in a Vite app itself—we're testing a Node.js CLI's `.cts` config support using Vitest, and the test fails due to this transpilation gap. In production, the CLI runs directly on Node.js, so `.cts` files work correctly.

The actual problematic line is [here](https://github.com/vivliostyle/vivliostyle-cli/blob/40b4cdecfd409207bd6e4271d839296e681eea69/src/config/load.ts#L62). When this dynamic `import()` is executed in Vitest (Vite's SSR mode), it goes through Vite's module resolution. Also note that `.cjs` files work correctly since they are plain JavaScript and don't require transpilation. The issue is specific to `.cts` files which contain TypeScript syntax.

I'm also experiencing almost the exact same issue:
In one of my projects, I could easily obtain a `RollupOutput` using the `.build` method. I then performed some processing on the code provided by RollupOutput before writing it to files.
However, when I tried to switch from a `single build` to `continuous watch`, I found that it was impossible to obtain `RollupOutput` no matter what I did.

After I continued to dive deeper into debugging the Rollup code, I discovered that this issue might not be resolvable only through Vite. This is because, in watch mode, Rollup does not pass any RollupOutput to any of its watcher events.

----
the key code is here:
https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/watch/watch.ts#L213

First, `.result` provided in the `BUNDLE_END` event is indeed the result from rollup; it implements the `RollupBuild` interface.

Then `RollupBuild` interface provides two functions, [**`generate()`**](https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/rollup/rollup.ts#L119) and [**`write()`**](https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/rollup/rollup.ts#L127), to produce a `RollupOutput`. These two functions are essentially the same, except for the first parameter `isWrite` being different when they call [`handleGenerateWrite()`](https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/rollup/rollup.ts#L190).

When `skipWrite` is not true, the code uses an await call to `result.write()` to generate and write the code to files. It's precisely here that they, surprisingly, do not pass the `RollupOutput` generated by `result.write()` to the `BUNDLE_END` event.

When `skipWrite` is true, neither `generate()` nor `write()` are called, making it even more impossible for a RollupOutput to exist.

----
It's evident that this piece of code, including the `skipWrite` config, fails to cover the scenario of "generating without writing".

If it were up to me, I would change `skipWrite` to a configuration option more like `afterRollup: 'write' | 'generate' | false`.

Furthermore, I would save the result of either `result.generate()` or `result.write()` and include it in the `BUNDLE_END` event.

## Case Study

Here is a related problem that I just dealt with. For context, I need my app to be polyfilled for Chrome 49 and Safari 13.1.

Initially, I did not set `modernTarget`, but did set `target` and `build.target` to their respective equivalent syntaxes of Chrome 49 and Safari 13.1
- I got a polyfilled legacy bundle that worked as expected for Chrome 49, but Safari 13.1 was loading the modern bundle, and it was not polyfilled.
- Got warnings that `build.target` was being overridden by `modernTarget`, even though I didn't set it.
- There were legacy and modern bundles, but only legacy polyfills

It took me a minute to realize that if modern bundles are enabled (they are by default), then the boundary between the modern and legacy bundles is _Native ESM + native ESM dynamic import + import.meta_, no matter what the targets are set to. I also realized that the value of `modernTarget` is _always_ applied to my app, including if it still has the default value, and regardless of the value `build.target`.

By default, `modernPolyfills` is false. In order to polyfill Safari 13.1, I need to polyfill my modern bundle by giving `modernPolyfills` an appropriate value. The legacy bundle will never load in Safari 13.1 if `renderModernChunks` is true, because Safari 12 is the earliest Safari to support native ESM, native ESM dynamic import, and import.meta. If I set `modernPolyfills` to `true` ([not recommended](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#modernpolyfills)), then Babel will use all the [default(?)] `modernTarget` browsers, compared to what features are detected in my code (plugin-legacy [uses `useBuiltIns: 'usage'`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/ad5b3bf6f3ad7b24886718c5f5de32eee923ae11/packages/plugin-legacy/src/index.ts#L595)), to get a bunch of polyfills that cover every edge case. I think _most_ of the modern polyfills are redundant, which, I imagine, is why the devs recommend not doing that. For me, that was 58 polyfills for modern, compared to 81 polyfills for legacy. The easy way to see which polyfills are used is by running `DEBUG=vite:legacy pnpm build` with `modernPolyfills: true`.

For now, I still need to decide if I want to 
- just leave in the extra polyfills. Most of them are not cutting edge features, and babel is using `useBuiltIns: 'usage'`, so _something_ in that default browser list wants these polyfills _for my code_
- check each polyfill in the modern bundle against caniuse, and manually include the appropriate polyfills (assuming it's detecting some edge cases that I will likely never see - e.g. `Symbol: description` in iOS 12.1).
- use cloudflare's polyfill service
- do a single legacy build for all browsers
- modify my code to not use the features that require polyfills

So there are definitely some fuzzy bits where the config experience could be improved, and/or the docs could be fleshed out a bit. @nulladdict -I bumped into annoying target syntax too, and also found the unsetting of build.target to feel backwards.

> The ideal solution is for oxc, rolldown and then vite to support functionality that plugin-env provides. This way users can use oxc-based polyfill detection and entirely avoid plugin-legacy for modern build

Love this. Hopefully we get here. If we are very lucky, this will also work for legacy workers.

But, for now, I think my experience with this has some answers to @nulladdict 's lingering questions that might also be useful for others or for adding to the docs. Depending on what nulladdict finds in their investigation, I could do a PR to update docs later.


## Missing Answers

> if I don't set the option would build.target still be replaced by some default?

Yes. `build.target` is always replaced by `modernTarget` when using plugin-legacy, which currently has the default setting of `'edge>=79, firefox>=67, chrome>=64, safari>=12, chromeAndroid>=64, iOS>=12'`. If you set `modernTarget` to something else, `build.target` will be replaced by that. 

Additionally, I _think_ `build.cssTarget` will also inherit those values for the modern bundle. For sure, it will always be set to `'chrome61'` for the legacy bundle.

> won't build.target fallback to its default value?

No. The plugin [manually overrides build.target](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/ad5b3bf6f3ad7b24886718c5f5de32eee923ae11/packages/plugin-legacy/src/index.ts#L240C9-L248C10) after the config is loaded (`configResolved` hook(s)), but before each build/bundle (`generateBundle` hook(s)).

UNLESS you are wondering if it will fallback to its default before another plugin runs after plugin legacy? In that case.. maybe? I'm not sure about that. But subsequent plugins will be running after the code is built and bundled, so I don't imagine many cases where that will matter, right? I don't really know.

> if I want to both render legacy chunks and add modern polyfills what do I do?

Populate [modernPolyfills](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#modernpolyfills) with core-js 3 specifiers, and/or [additionalModernPolyfills](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#additionalmodernpolyfills) with paths to manually installed polyfills, or set to `true`.

Usually, you should not change the default `modernTargets` if you also want a legacy bundle. If you change any browsers in this list to a lower version than what they are now, nothing will change, because any lower version will load the legacy bundle anyway (`nomodule` etc). If you change it to anything higher, then there will be a gap of supported versions between the legacy bundle and whatever higher version you specify. That might be ok in your case, but would generally be undesireable.

e.g. 
- your code uses [Array.flatMap](https://caniuse.com/array-flat) (Chrome 69+)
- default `modernTarget` is >=Chrome 64
- you change `modernTarget` to >=Chrome 107 (vite's new default `build.target`)

The bit of built code that uses flatMap works in browsers <=Chrome63, and >=Chrome69 (where `flatMap` was introduced), but not any browser in between (i.e. Chrome 64-68).

I suppose if we wanted the modernTargets threshold to change, we would have to write a different detector. [Currently it is](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/ad5b3bf6f3ad7b24886718c5f5de32eee923ae11/packages/plugin-legacy/src/snippets.ts#L10C1-L10C125) 

```js
export const detectModernBrowserDetector: string = `import.meta.url;import("_").catch(()=>1);(async function*(){})().next()`

```

I think I can answer those questions. I think your questions are partly answered in the [vite build docs](https://vite.dev/guide/build). Plugin-legacy docs assume you are familiar with that already 

> 1. Suppose we're using a newer target such as baseline-widely-available or baseline 2021 or something similar. Does that mean that we do not need to use polyfills (either using a 3rd party or using @vitejs/plugin-legacy) at all?

Correct (mostly). You won't need `plugin-legacy` to cover browsers that vite can target natively (https://vite.dev/guide/build#browser-compatibility), which is to say, any browser target that esbuild can cover by transforming your codebase using syntax lowering without polyfills. So at some point, it depends a bit on what javascript features you are using in your code. But vite/esbuild _should_ throw an error at build time if there is a javascript feature in your codebase that can't be transformed for your target ([esbuild target docs](https://esbuild.github.io/api/#target)). If that happens, then you either need to get rid of it, or polyfill it. Plugin-legacy is just 1 option for polyfilling (but it's definitely the easiest).

> 2. And suppose we're using an older target, so old that those browser do not support native ESM. I think we need to use @vitejs/plugin-legacy here? For browsers that do support native ESM, the polyfills won't be loaded right? Does that mean those browsers do not need the polyfills? (which is question 1 again)

`plugin-legacy` makes 2 bundles by default, the threshold is `Native ESM + native ESM dynamic import + import.meta`, which translates to `edge>=79, firefox>=67, chrome>=64, safari>=12, chromeAndroid>=64, iOS>=12`. Any browser below these will load the legacy bundle, which is automatically polyfilled based on your target. If you need polyfills in the modern target, then you can manually set those with the `modernPolyfills` option, as described [in the docs](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#modernpolyfills).

Since esbuild throws an error if it can't transform something, before you even attempt to use plugin-legacy, I would set your target in the regular vite build options, and try building your app. If you get no errors, then you should be good to go! Obviously, you should still test in your target browsers to be sure.

Fixed by #21319

This is also related to / duplicate of nuxt/nuxt#21041

> **Root Cause:**

The issue is in the parsing regex in packages/vite/src/node/plugins/workerImportMetaUrl.ts (line 212).
When Prettier formats new URL(..., import.meta.url) across multiple lines, it adds a trailing comma after import.meta.url:
Prettier formats long paths like this:

```
  const worker = new Worker(
    new URL(
      "../some-loooooooooooooooooong-file-path.js",
      import.meta.url,   // ← trailing comma
    ),
    { type: "module" },
  )
```

The Worker plugin's regex expects:
`  import.meta.url )`

  But Prettier produces:
`  import.meta.url, )`



> **Comparison with Asset Plugin**

Interestingly, the asset plugin (assetImportMetaUrl.ts) already handles this correctly:
Asset plugin regex (line 63-64) - WORKS ✅

```
  \bnew\s+URL\s*\(\s*('[^']+'|"[^"]+"|`[^`]+`)\s*,\s*import\.meta\.url\s*(?:,\s*)?\)/dg
                                                                          ^^^^^^^^^^
                                                             handles optional trailing comma
```

Worker plugin regex (line 211-212) - BROKEN ❌
```
\bnew\s+(?:Worker|SharedWorker)\s*\(\s*(new\s+URL\s*\(\s*('[^']+'|"[^"]+"|`[^`]+`)\s*,\s*import\.meta\.url\s*\))/dg
                                                                                   missing (?:,\s*)?  ^^^

```



> **Try**

Add (?:,\s*)? before the closing ) in the Worker parsing regex to handle optional trailing comma:

I wouldn't handle them in prod! 😅 At least for the approach I've taken with CSP, there are two distinct plugins which implement CSP differently—an `apply: 'serve'` plugin which uses nonces (useful in dev), and an `apply: 'build'` plugin which computes JS hashes (useful to minimize transformation in production server), injects `integrity` attributes to `<script>` tags, and emits a full set of hashes to a separate file (to be consumed by the production server). This separation seems to make sense because during `vite dev`, Vite is doing the serving, but in `vite build`, the serving is done by the production server (e.g., Express, GitHub Pages, etc.), so there is a natural asymmetry around which entity is responsible for emitting HTTP response headers in either case.

But if one is forced to use use nonces in production, I believe the plugin must emit a placeholder during build in `transformIndexHtml` (e.g., `<script nonce="__NONCE_PLACEHOLDER__">`)—which requires only the `html` parameter; no other context required. When the Vite build output is served to customers, the HTML files must be transformed at serve time to inject the nonce generated by the server.

> e.g. you can patch res.end = () => { /* do something and call res.end again */ } and inject your CSP handling there too.

This is an interesting hack/patch! Will need to try it.

> (Also to be clear, I'm not opposed to adding it yet. Trying to understand its usecase as transformIndexHtml also has many caveats today)

Thanks for clarifying your present feeling on the matter! I believe I may have run into one such caveat with `transformIndexHtml` in my implementation of the `apply: 'build'` plugin which computes hashes... As it turned out, `transformIndexHtml` runs _before_ some final JS transformations during build—namely `postImportMapHook()`:

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/055d2b86b0543a7c1a2a4d5bc7298af62bc51fa7/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/html.ts#L288-L293

As a result, if the JS chunk referenced from HTML were to be hashed in `transformIndexHtml`, its content would be different from the final output, and therefore the hashes wouldn't match. To work around this, the plugin uses a `generateBundle` hook with `order: 'post'` to defer hashing JS chunks until _after_ `postImportMapHook()` runs.

Zooming out a bit, the original thought behind exposing `req` and `res` within `transformIndexHtml` was not to upset the balance between build and serve modes, but rather to attempt to improve the ergonomics of working with the _current request/response_ during `vite dev/preview` only, without having any effect on `vite build`. By contrast, during build, Vite already runs the rich set of Rollup hooks, so the ergonomics of working with the current module/chunk/bundle already seem quite flexible and extensible by comparison (e.g., given the `generateBundle` example above).

We also ran into this issue at my company.

## Context

Prior to using vite, we used another build server via http with a url like `http://localhost:9002`. There are still a lot of legacy occurrences of this URL throughout our company: links generated in CI, browser history and bookmarks, etc. One of the main issues that keeps cropping up is that devs will enter the bare `localhost` into their address bar and it will autocomplete to the http version.

We want to continue using the same port so there isn't really an option to run a small side-car server to redirect.

## Our workaround

We are considering implementing the same approach as described above: a small tcp proxy that redirects http → https, and delegates https → the vite server. This works, but then we have to explain to devs to avoid calling `vite dev` which is a bummer.

Not sure if it matters for your app, but you should use `optimizeDeps.entries: ['./src/all.js']` (add any relevant html entrypoints if needed for crawling) instead of `optimizeDeps.include`, since the latter means bundling `src/all.js` entirely with esbuild. We only want to crawl and bundle the crawled files' dependencies. Some stats on my machine:
Scan time Bundle time
optimizeDeps.include 256ms 6000ms
optimizeDeps.entries 3981ms 1358ms
If you do have `optimizeDeps.include` misconfigured, you can switch to this and offload the timing to the scanner. The scanning time can be easily bypassed by manually specifying the deps in `optimizeDeps.include` yourself, and then set `optimizeDeps.entries` to an empty array. --- If the config is right, I guess we can consider adding information of the prebundling progress. The reason I'm a bit hesitant with adding a progress bar is because rendering it requires continuous updates, and it can interfere with logs from plugins or debug logs when that happens. They're ways around this I suppose by delay showing it, or only log a line about "taking longer than usual". Also, there's not a lot of progress information we can show, especially for the esbuild bundling. We pass the dependency entrypoints to esbuild, and then wait for its output. Hooking to the esbuild bundling hooks to log progress would probably only slow it down. I'd like to hear what others on the team thinks about this request too.

If you are using NPM, then configure NPM to not auto-install optional peer dependencies.
Add `omit=optional` to your `.npmrc` file.
Then uninstall and reinstall Vite, which will first remove Vite and its dependencies from your package lock file, and then will only add Vite back with the _required_ dependencies. After that, manually install `sass` and don't install `sass-embedded`.

Sadly, NPM is a bit nuts and configuring optional dependencies to be omitted and then doing `npm un sass-embedded` when it's already installed, **won't work**. (Probably because the lock file still instructs that it's non-optional.)

Is it possible for a package to dynamically change it's dev dependencies based on the platform, or have platform-specific dependencies? I could not figure out how to use a package override to completely replace one package with another.

The existence of these two `sass` packages will create headaches for anyone developing on an unsupported platform unless every consumer checks that `sass-embedded` works. I can see everyone legitimately saying it's a different package's problem.

> Is it possible for a package to dynamically change it's dev dependencies based on the platform, or have platform-specific dependencies? I could not figure out how to use a package override to completely replace one package with another.

Yes. It's possible, but not dynamically in the sense of at the level of the dependent package.
Declaring the supported platforms is managed at the level of the dependency package itself.
Which means you also can't override anything about how the dependency is registered with the dependent, to make it vary by platform, where those instructions are absent or misconfigured.

See also https://github.com/npm/rfcs/discussions/120 which was meant to tackle this problem.
(Specifically by introducing `platformDependencies`.)

Development Mode (vite dev):
Vite serves files with native ES modules
The browser's native module system handles the imports
The browser's module loader sees broke:// as a valid URL protocol and tries to resolve it and throws cors error
Since broke isn't a registered protocol, it fails

Production Mode (vite preview):
Vite has already processed and bundled all imports during the build
All aliases are resolved to their final paths
The browser never sees the original broke:// protocol, 



The $ in $okay:// makes it an invalid protocol in URLs, which is why it gets passed through Vite's transform pipeline correctly in both dev and production.

Thanks for the quick response and the detailed explanation, bluwy. Your analysis makes perfect sense.

You're right that `dotenv` could be a solution in a custom script. However, the core issue arises when a user directly runs the `vite build --mode production` command. In this scenario, Bun pre-populates `process.env` from `.env.development` *before* the Vite CLI even starts executing. By the time Vite's internal `loadEnv` is called, it's too late – `process.env` already contains the wrong values, and Vite correctly prioritizes them. A user can't inject `dotenv` into Vite's internal build process to fix this.

This leads to a "silent failure" where the build succeeds but contains incorrect production variables, which can be very difficult to debug.

My goal with this issue was less about asking for a complex code fix and more about raising awareness. Given that Bun is gaining popularity as a runtime, other users will inevitably encounter this.

Perhaps the most practical solution would be to add a note to the Vite documentation? A small section on a "Common Issues" page or in the guide about using different runtimes, warning about Bun's default `.env` loading behavior and recommending the `bun --env-file=.env.production` or `NODE_ENV=production bun ...` workarounds would be immensely helpful for the community.
Yeah I think docs is probably the best way forward too. Maybe a short info block at https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode.html#env-files explaining the issue for Bun users.

Webpack has a more complex approach for determining CSS Modules via `modules.auto`,
https://webpack.js.org/loaders/css-loader/#auto
Which supports:
```ts
type auto =
  | boolean
  | RegExp
  | ((
      resourcePath: string,
      resourceQuery: string,
      resourceFragment: string
    ) => boolean);
```

* `boolean` — enable/disable for all files
* `RegExp` — enable for files matching a pattern
* `function(resourcePath, resourceQuery, resourceFragment)` — custom logic per file

```ts

It seems a workaround is to use `target: new URL('/', 'http://localhost:3000')` instead of `target: new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')`.

I think this is an expected behavior change.

`http-proxy` does not receive `URL`, but receives the legacy [`url.Url`](https://nodejs.org/api/url.html#legacy-urlobject). `http-proxy-3` receives `URL` as well.
`new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')` is an instance of `URL` with some properties that overlaps with `url.Url`.
- For `http-proxy`, `new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')` was treated as `{ pathname: '/api', host: 'localhost:3000', ...otherProperties }` and `http-proxy` doesn't use the `pathname` property (it only reads the `path` property). So it was treated as `http://localhost:3000`.
- For `http-proxy-3`, `new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')` is treated as an instance of `URL` and `http-proxy-3` uses the `pathname` property. So it is treated as `http://localhost:3000/api`.

Usually this is handled by only setting `resolve.noExternal: true` during build only if it's needed to bundle the deps.

I gave this a go, but it looks like `resolve.noExternal: false` doesn't work well with the way Deno resolves modules. If set to `false` it seems like vite bypasses the plugin system entirely and assumes that it can use the node resolution algorithm for bare specifiers. This is not correct in the Deno world as there are no guarantees how the `node_modules` folder is laid out. It might be using the global cache dir or the local `node_modules` directory.

Disabling that option also breaks custom aliases in Deno for the same reason as bare specifiers are not passed through the plugin system anymore. JSR imports are also broken (again because they're not passed through the plugin system anymore).

The way resolution in Deno works is that it's important _where_ resolution is kicked of. It doesn't work like in node where it just bubbles up the directory tree to find a matching `node_modules/<pkg>` directory. It seems like this is assumed though internally in vite.

Vite `v7.x` and above use the new `crypto.hash()` API, which is only available in:

Node.js v20.19.0+

   bash:
   nvm install 22.16.0
   nvm use 22.16.0
   

3. Reinstalled dependencies:

   bash : 
   rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
   npm install

In case it's helpful, here is the desired workflow:

1. Build docker image
2. Docker build container performs vite build
3. Docker build container copies static serving files to Nginx image to finish building production container
4. Production container is run in production environment with env variables set to their desired values
5. Production container initialization script writes those env variables to the proper env/json/whatever file before serving starts
6. App can use config values provided by the production container rather than the build container

Currently, step 2 causes production replacement to occur in the build container, meaning that the process can't change the env values from that point on. To use different env values for the container, you'd have to build the container again, meaning you'd need a different container image for every environment.

Vite can not correctly deal with dependency chains of mixed ESM and CJS:

App -> ESM works
App -> CJS works
App -> ESM -> ESM works
App -> ESM -> CJS fails

There is a suggested workaround via [optimizeDeps.include](https://vitejs.dev/config/dep-optimization-options.html#optimizedeps-exclude) that each module consumer would have to add, so it's far from a usable solution.

The only reliable workaround is to bundle your ESM modules that have CJS dependencies themselves, but that comes at the cost of  dependency duplication.

Considering that:
1. I can't think of an efficient way to support this feature.
    - The packages are excluded by esbuild because they're external.
    - Most of the external packages used by `vite.config.*` don't (and shouldn't) require transpilation
    - It's already a configuration file, we don't want to introduce another option to configure the loading logic of the configuration file.
2. The use case is quite rare. The logic in the configuration file is usually not very complex. Even if it is extracted to a separate package, I think it's acceptable to be written in plain JS or processed by an additional run of `tsc`.

So this feature would be a low priority for the team.
But feel free to open a PR if you can find a better and efficient way to handle this use case.

If you want to use a monorepo/workspace with typescript, you should set it up correctly using [project references](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/project-references.html) with compilerOptions `composite: true`, since you can't import an untranspiled `.ts` file in a transpiled module. Every module (like a plugin) you import into `vite.config.ts` is already transpiled to `js`.
Even without `vite`, the projects need to be referenced. While developing you should use [ts-node](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ts-node) or [tsx](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tsx), so you don't need to rebuild the files all the time.

I think there are possibly two separate issues being described by different users/teams in this thread:
1. failed to fetch after a new deployment where the old version was deleted from the server
  - in this case, attempting to load the resource referenced by the error is expected to fail, it has been deleted
2. failed to fetch that occurs somewhat randomly
  - in this case, attempting to load the resource succeeds

For people experiencing issue 1., the solution is to organise your deployments so that old versions aren't deleted immediately. Doing a deployment of new app code doesn't mean that all users running your app in their browser will update immediately (unless you force it somehow).

For those users who still have an older version running in their browser (lets say `index.123.js`), navigating to routes that load chunks dynamically will always reference the chunk that was current when they loaded your app (ie `home.123.js`), and this is correct. You don't want the user getting half of their chunks with new app code and half with old, this would lead to very hard to debug issues. If you delete those chunks while the user is still navigating around the app, you will hit this error when they change routes and try to load a chunk they haven't loaded yet.

For users that load the app after a deployment, `index.html` will reference a new `index.456.js` chunk that references all the other chunks that are consistent with that version (ie `home.456.js` if there are also changes in that chunk). The only difference is which version was referenced by `index.html` when the user loaded the tab.

If you keep a manifest of each deployment, and your instrumentation/logging includes the "version" of the app users are using, you should be able to figure out how long old versions are still used. My team has seen users still operating in the same tab they loaded a month ago without updating, so we keep all our built assets deployed for a long time. If you want to force users to reload when a new version is deployed, that's a whole piece of engineering in itself.

This is irrelevant. Vite does not set `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` tag. It only injects `<meta property="csp-nonce">` tag for internal usage.

> * If you generate a random `nonce` both for the header and for the `html.cspNonce` option, on the `vite.config.js`, Vite would read this file twice at different times to generate one or the other, entirely breaking your site by not having a matching nonce everywhere.

> * Even worse, if you build a SPA with `vite build`, the `nonce` will be generated only once, which is not secure at all, as it should be different for every request. Not to mention that `nonce` is not compatible with static content which is usually cached.

Hi @sapphi-red, 

Thanks for the quick reply. It helped me understand the mechanism much better.

I agree that:
- The `<meta property="csp-nonce">` is for internal use, and that any use of CSP's nonce feature should be complemented by setting the appropriate HTTP header (`Content-Security-Policy` with the corresponding nonce value.)
- The `html.cspNonce` is meant to hold a placeholder that is replaced server-side.
- The docs as they stand are clear on all fronts.

Based on this, I think the core of my suggestion might be adapted to still provide a better docs experience:

My concern is that the typical reader will often have an SPA (maybe with some traditional-server deployment) use-case in mind.

Even if the user were to implement the `http.nonce` placeholder, and replace it programatically on each request, I think this workflow is at odds with the typical static-file hosting of SPA. Particularly, a nonce would be in direct conflict with Vite's cache strategy of `Cache-Control: max-age=31535999,immutable` .

So a reader might:
1. Incorrectly build with a "static nonce."
2. Implement it properly, but at the cost of HTTP caching.

I believe the docs could offer a tip explaining the issues with nonce-based CSP and static sites, and maybe recommend a hash-based CSP approach, like the one used by `vite-plugin-csp-guard`.

We discussed this feature in a recent team meeting and we decided that the best path forward is:
- Vite will leave import maps definitions untouched.
- A new [`external` config option](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/6582) will be implemented, that allows to define that an id is external for both dev and build.
- Users will need to add all the entry ids from import maps to this new `external` config option.

Vite has a single module graph for its server. If you have two modules imported by different HTML entry points, they will be a single module node in graph. Vite could automatically read the import map and respect it without `external` but that will be a big change in the conceptual model of Vite dev. Every module should start having a `?entry=path.html` query for example. We are also able to request a module in isolation, but this will break. Having the entries of the import map as `external` avoids these issues.

I have created a plugin to solve this issue during development, until official support is implemented:

https://github.com/MilanKovacic/vite-plugin-externalize-dependencies

Hi @lozinsky, @sapphi-red!  

I've looked into this issue and would like to contribute a fix.  

From my analysis:
- The issue occurs because `revokeObjectURL` is called in the `finally` block, invalidating the Blob URL before WebKit workers can use it.
- WebKit requires the Blob URL to remain valid for the worker's lifecycle.
- Based on @sapphi-red’s suggestion, moving the `revokeObjectURL` call **inside the worker script** should resolve this issue.

I will update [`vite/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/worker.ts`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/worker.ts) to:
1. Remove the `revokeObjectURL` call from the `finally` block.
2. Ensure it's called inside the worker script instead.
3. Test the fix in Playwright WebKit.

I'll start working on this and submit a PR soon. Let me know if there's any feedback before I proceed! 🚀

All package managers will not install optional peer dependencies by default. They are optional. The issue is that they're fetching metadata for them even if they're not installed.

> and for users to be required to explicitely install them.

That's already how it is today. I don't really understand the proposal here. We cannot just remove them from `package.json`, unless you want us to remove CSS preprocessors support entirely and break the entire ecosystem.

> The issue is that they're fetching metadata for them even if they're not installed.

Yeah, pnpm (and possibly others?) fetching metadata sounds like a bug in those package managers.

> We cannot just remove them from package.json, unless you want us to remove CSS preprocessors support entirely and break the entire ecosystem.

At which point does the optional peer dependency become relevant? The [docs](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#css-pre-processors) already specify the user has to `npm add` preprocessors. What does the peerDependency actually achieve in such a case?

It declares the additional dependencies that vite can import, and the versions that Vite supports. In a strict installation, packages can only import the declared deps and peer deps. You can't import some arbitrary dep, and if it somehow works, potentially getting the wrong version. An optional peer deps means additionally package managers don't have to install it and vite can function normally with it not installed, until the user manually installs it.

I'd suggest reading some resources/docs on how optional peer deps work.

But why does vite need to import them in first place? Wouldn't it be better if CSS preprocessors were plugins? Given that CSS preprocessors are mostly obsolete today, I'd appreciate them being moved to plugins.

I'm also in favor of moving them to separate plugins so the main package stays lean. Not sure how feasible it is but given the problems around peer dependencies, I'm not entirely sold on keeping them around. Though it makes sense that something similar like this happening is unlikely.

Ok so in summary we have two potential action points:

1. pnpm should not attempt to fetch metadata for packages it's not going to install (I'm not going to file a issue because I don't use pnpm)
2. vite to potentially extract the CSS preprocessors to plugins (in a future major version)

I don't really think moving them as plugins is going to help much. It causes more friction for users who want to use CSS preprocessors and isn't worth the effort to have everyone migrate again. This really seem like an edge case in package managers that should be fixed there. I'm happy to be proven wrong though but again, optional peer dependencies are normal patterns in libraries and I don't think there's a reason they should be avoided.

I just ran into this issue when setting up a project and had some commented out code that included `</head>` above the 'real' and uncommented out `</head>`

For an even sillier example that breaks: `<!doctype html><title>The <header> element</title>`
Vite will mistake the text `<header>` inside that title for a `<head>` tag.

I alleviated a similar issue a while back in [hugo](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/commit/9dc608084b73f04c146351cbe8d1b2f41058e8ba) and found the same problem in [VS Code](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-livepreview/issues/711#issuecomment-2807935577) a couple weeks ago. Haven't found the time make a PR there or here yet, but feel free to steal the code I wrote there.

The problem is threefold:
-   Using regular expressions to naively **search** for tags within an arbitrary HTML fragment is impossible. Many constructs can be nested and hold arbitrary text that looks like tags, so determining if a piece of code is actually a tag is impossible without context.
-   Beyond that, using regular expressions in the form `/<tagname[^>]*>/` to match entire tags isn't reliable. This leads to injections after `<header>` instead of `<head>` or inside an attribute value that contains a `>`.
-   Scanning through the whole document for a specific injection point, then falling back to searching for another injection point, is inefficient and increases the risks of false positives.

I recommend scanning the document from the start, and only reading past whitespace, comments, the doctype, the html tag and the head tag. HTML comments cannot be nested so they can be consumed reliably, and the risk of encountering a breaking attribute on the `<html>` or `<head>` tags are low.

As you know, files that is not included in the `exports` field cannot be accessed via `import`. This is how Node.js works.

If package "a" accesses like that, package `a` is broken and it should be fixed on the package "a" side.
If package "b" added such an `exports` field in a minor or patch version, that is a error in that package. Because adding that is a breaking change.
If package "b" added it in a major version, then package "a" won't have a problem because package "a" would still be able to use the old version.

If you need to workaround it, you can patch the package "a"'s package.json to be:
```json
  "exports": {
    "./*.js": "./*.js"
  }
```
You can also make a plugin for it if that's preferred.

I don't think Vite should allow non-standard things.

Thanks for the fast reply and it is very inspirational!

> If package "b" added it in a major version, then package "a" won't have a problem because package "a" would still be able to use the old version.

That’s exactly where the issue arises. Even if package “b” introduces the exports field in a major version, as long as package “b” doesn’t change its internal file structure, package “a”‘s outdated build tool won’t even notice. Since the tool doesn’t recognize the exports field, it unintentionally bypasses these new restrictions, making the breaking change effectively invisible to package “a”.

From this perspective, maybe it seems more like a design drawback of the `exports` field?

I'm totally fine with the decision of sticking with standard things only. I believe that is one important reason of Vite's success today.

In dev, Vite currently handles modules imported as workers or imported from workers in the same way as if they were imported from normal modules.
This is because there were no way to detect whether a module was imported from a worker or not. But now that the `Sec-Fetch-Dest` header is available, we can detect that a module is imported from a worker.
With that we should be able to process modules imported from workers differently from modules imported from normal modules.

After that is implemented, we can add resolve options that are specific to workers or add `worker` condition by default (https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/7439).

`bufferedError` is set to null on a new connection, but that races with the code that sets `bufferedError` when sending the payload. At the time it sends out the error, there's typically only one of the clients connected. This comment https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/c5b71915099cfbc15447a166f35620fa0e05c023/packages/vite/src/node/server/ws.ts#L344-L348

Seems to suggest it was intentional, given the singular "client". This was introduced in https://github.com/vitejs/vite/commit/23016ca4d9bf88d5c5157ca9536b18f2e3ab3c4b, and I don't see any indication of exactly why we need to set `bufferedError` to `null` there.

While Vite can support `this.fs` (https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/20301), it is currently unclear whether the `fs` option can be supported.

In the future, [Vite will migrate to Rolldown](https://vite.dev/guide/rolldown.html), and Rolldown may not be able to support the `fs` option.

<details>
<summary>fs option support in Rolldown</summary>

File system calls in oxc_resolver (a dep used in Rolldown) are sync. To support the `fs` option, we would need to either make these calls async or work around it by using `tokio::block_in_place`. However, it's unclear whether this would work reliably and whether the perf degration would be acceptable.

</details>

Until we're confident that the `fs` option can be implemented in Rolldown, I think Vite should avoid supporting it.

Here’s the spec (with comments about the case in this issue in italics):

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#prepare-the-script-element

> To prepare the script element given a script element el:
>
> ...
>
> 35. If el's type is "classic" and el has a src attribute, or el's type is "module": _(type is "module")_
>
>     1. Assert: el's result is "uninitialized". _(it is)_
>
>     2. If el has an async attribute or el's force async is true: _(not async, not force async – read the rest of the spec about that)_
>
>        ...
>
>     3. Otherwise, if el is not parser-inserted: _(it IS parser-inserted)_
>
>        ...
>
>     4. Otherwise, if el has a defer attribute or el's type is "module": _(type is "module")_
>
>         1. [Append](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list-append) el to its parser document's [list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#list-of-scripts-that-will-execute-when-the-document-has-finished-parsing).
>
>         2. Set el's steps to run when the result is ready to the following: set el's ready to be parser-executed to true. (The parser will handle executing the script.)

https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list-append

> To append to a [list](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list) that is not an ordered set is to add the given item to the end of the list.

https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list

> A list is a specification type consisting of a finite **ordered sequence** of items.

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#list-of-scripts-that-will-execute-when-the-document-has-finished-parsing

> Each Document has a [list](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#list) of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing, which is a list of script elements, initially empty.

As far as I can tell:

- The browser keeps an **ordered list** of scripts to execute.
- The browser **appends** (adds to the end) of the list when it parses `<script type="module">`.

It makes sense that the execution order is defined. A big role of the HTML specification is to define how a document is supposed to work, so that implementations don’t have to disagree.

It appears that Vite deliberately strips the import attribute syntax:

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/3af02bde7e7f26889d5c0eb300219c43ed1293ad/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/importAnalysis.ts#L494-L497

Worth noting that import attributes are [supported by TypeScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-3.html#import-attributes) along with [native support in Chrome](https://caniuse.com/mdn-javascript_statements_import_import_attributes).

It would be great it `vite` could avoid adulterating the import syntax in my code so that the runtime itself can interpret what I authored.

The workaround right now:

```
// vite strips the type declaration syntax
import stylesheet from './demo-badge.css' with { type: 'css' };

// vite does not modify the syntax
const { default: stylesheet } = await import('./demo-badge.css', { with: { type: 'css' } });
```

Some prior comments on the topic:
* https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/12140#issuecomment-1440150314
* https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/10633#issuecomment-1534125299

As a first step toward solving this issue, I think it might be nice to have an option to disable the current CSS runtime behavior entirely.

In other words, `*.css` files would be treated the same as any non-JS file type (e.g. `*.mdx`, `.tsx`, etc.), and plugins would be able to transform the CSS files to JS as needed.

This would fit the usecase of the [LWC framework](https://lwc.dev/) – in LWC, importing a CSS file returns a function:

```js
import stylesheet from './styles.css' // imports a function that returns a string
```

Currently, this functionality doesn't work in Vite even with our Rollup plugin (`@lwc/rollup-plugin`), due to Vite's default handling of CSS. (I have [a minimal repro](https://github.com/nolanlawson/lwc-vitest-demo/tree/test-styles-rendered) of this issue using Vitest.)

Unfortunately, the `?inline` or `with { type: 'css' }` solutions would not work for us, because it would be a breaking change for existing components (which do not use such syntax when importing stylesheets).

Potentially, our Rollup plugin could apply these transformations itself (to the `.js` files that are importing `.css` files), but I wonder if a more generic "disable the current CSS behavior" option would be a simpler solution for other web component frameworks in general.

TSConfig `paths` only works for TypeScript / JavaScript modules (semantically). We need the alias for all kinds of resources. 
So I think it would be confusing to use `paths` exclusively.
The feature should explicitly support (and validate it works with) a tsconfig.json with the `extends` keyword to import a tsconfig.base.json that has paths defined in the base file.

Adding some notes from [#10063: tsconfig paths do not work in vite.config.ts](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/10063), which was closed in favor of this issue.

In addition to the recommended functionality of `vite-tsconfig-paths`, which only works for the project being built, it would also be ideal to have `paths` aliases accessible within the execution of `vite.config.ts` itself.

While I'd like to see first-class support for this as well, unfortunately tsconfig paths and `resolve.alias` are not a one-to-one behaviour.

- tsconfig paths are a lot more lenient and involves multiple resolves / filesystem access to match the resolved path
- `resolve.alias` is stricter where the first regex match will immediately replace and return the resolved path (only string manipulation)

tldr; a lot of people use `NODE_ENV` when they shouldn't. It's a common (anti)pattern. The updated docs in https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/14978 do a good job of clarifying the relationship between `NODE_ENV` and `mode`. 

...it's probably not the responsibility of the framework to tell us why it doesn't do something it shouldn't be doing. They also don't use `var` for every variable, but they don't tell us why they don't. If `mode` and/or `NODE_ENV` is something you need, be sure you know why you need it?

---

Vite controls `mode`. It does not control `NODE_ENV`. `NODE_ENV` is not vite-specific - it is an old paradigm, I think started by expressjs. It is also not official, but is so common that [npm optionally reads it](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-install) to decide whether to install `devDependencies`. pnpm fairly recently [stopped reading it](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/8827) (compare [v9](https://pnpm.io/9.x/cli/install#--prod--p) to [v10](https://pnpm.io/cli/install#--prod--p) install docs). Officially, node [calls it an antipattern](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/nodejs-the-difference-between-development-and-production).

`NODE_ENV` - vite reads this and interprets it to set `.DEV/.PROD` _at build time_. But it doesn't its own change behaviour based on that value, and doesn't overwrite `NODE_ENV` automagically (it respects all existing `process.env` values). Other libraries, or even hosting services, may depend on it, so you can't just get rid of it. Any script or command could change NODE_ENV at or before build or load time - there is a chance it could be set to something unexpected.

`mode` - vite is (obviously) not your application - it's a dev server and build tool, so it properly needs to differentiate environments, even if you agree about `NODE_ENV` being an antipattern. But you should still be cautious about how you use it IMHO. `mode` causes vite to load different environment variable files, is available only inside your app, and gets interpreted at build-time. It is the explicitly set mode of your app, and not necessarily the environment in which it's running. 

`mode` is part of `import.meta.env`, which is interpreted at build-time and values cannot be modified externally once built. `NODE_ENV` is part of `process.env` (by convention), and _can_ be modified at load time (this is probably why it's considered an antipattern to us inside your app - the same build could behave unexpectedly differently in different environments).

Some examples: you could create a vite build in dev, staging, or production mode (`vite build --mode <development/staging/production>`), all in a production environment (`NODE_ENV=production`). The example of changing the title is a good one - you might want your app to literally say the word "staging" in the title so that it's clear to QA that they are in the right place, but your build will be in a live, production-like environment (e.g. deployed to heroku or vercel or something). 

The `.env` files are a good example too. You might want different API end-points for different app modes (since vite loads different `.env` files based on mode, if they are available), but still deploy in production-like environment. Or, you might want to temporarily test your production end-points in the dev server. You can set vite's `mode` to production, even though your NODE_ENV might be development.
Afterthought - if people agree with me but still think that clarifying this is the responsibility of vite, I'd be game to work on adding some extra context to the docs.

I dug into this issue today. The reason why we had forced `keepNames: false` is due to https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/9164. If we reverted that, everyone's bundle size is likely to explode because treeshaking won't be working effectively (if they set `keepNames: true`).

I investigated the source of that issue and filed a feature request to esbuild that should fix it instead: https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/issues/3965. If that's resolved, we should be safe to revert the option.

(Note that if those are resolved, the source issue repro will generate a JS bundle rather than 0 JS, but it's less impactful in practice because treeshaking is still effective, just that it's not smart enough to reduce to 0 JS.)
But why do we need it during dev? 🤔
I guess we could allow it during dev, but build wouldn't be able to match it if we still set `keepNames: false` in build and would cause inconsistencies.

True, dev won’t catch the error and it will be hard to debug when it fails in production 😔

to add to this: there a lot of scenario that requires class names to be maintained (like if you are using decorators that tracks the name of the class), that gets 'mysteriously' broken by this behaviour.

forcing `keepNames: false` behind the scene is not transparent (users might find this only in prod when they minify the code) and the fact that it cannot be overridden leaves the user no choice but to use another minifier (terser).

I appreciate your concern about bundle size but to address that you are sacrificing build correctness and that does not sound right

> I guess we could allow it during dev, but build wouldn't be able to match it if we still set `keepNames: false` in build and would cause inconsistencies.

so don't enable it by default - presumably, people who enable this will know why they did that.

and if this is enabled in a production build, issue a warning/notice explaining why the build may be larger.

> to add to this: there a lot of scenario that requires class names to be maintained (like if you are using decorators that tracks the name of the class), that gets 'mysteriously' broken by this behaviour.

yes. 😌

in fact, the [esbuild docs](https://esbuild.github.io/api/#keep-names) pretty much tell all:

> minification renames symbols to reduce code size and **bundling sometimes need to rename symbols to avoid collisions**. That changes value of the name property for many of these cases. This is usually fine because the name property is normally only used for debugging. However, **some frameworks rely on the name property for registration and binding purposes.**

so the problem doesn't solely exist because of minification - bundling itself may require renaming, which can break things.

esbuild provides this feature, with whatever caveats it may have, for well documented reasons.

For the first point (`glob` is bundled):

Vite externalizes dependencies that are not possible to resolve from the application. In this case, `glob` is not a dependency of the application and does not exist in `node_modules/glob` and is externalized.
If you run `deno add -D npm:glob`, `glob` gets externalized.

It seems bun generates `node_modules/glob`, which is a [phantom dependency](https://rushjs.io/pages/advanced/phantom_deps/), a transitive dependency that are possible to resolve from the application. 

This is an expected behavior.

For the second point (`node:` prefix is lacking):

This is because `glob` has a import to `fs` without `node:`. Vite does not add or remove `node:` automatically.

I see some people are encountering this with `vite dev`. In that case, you should (1) connect the Chrome inspector to your Vite process and (2) pause the step debugger (do this shortly after starting the dev server and without loading anything in your browser). It's possible that you have a relatively complex circular directory symlink chain, and `readdirp` is being tricked into infinitely crawling those directories (but asynchronously, thereby avoiding a stack overflow). If the step debugger opens a `readdirp` file, you can be sure this is your issue. This is common if you're developing a chain of packages locally and linking one of them into your Vite project.

Using the `server.watch.ignored` option in Vite config, you can prevent `chokidar` (the file watcher that Vite uses) from watching the circular directory chain.

We have the same issue:

1. In `config`, start a listener and push its hostname to `allowedHosts`.
2. In `configureServer`, in `httpServer.on("listening")` callback, start forwarding to the HTTP server.
3. Never close the listener. 😕

`buildEnd`, `httpServer.on("close")`, etc. all seem to run on server restart as well as Vite exit, so if we use those, the server breaks on restart. We can only create the listener once, so we only want to dispose of it once when Vite is exiting.

Instead, what if could start my listener in `httpServer.on("listening")`, _then_ somehow push its hostname to Vite's `allowedHosts`?

Ideally, Vite would only use web standards such as `Request` and `Response` — which already cover a lot of what Vite needs. That said, there is still a gap between web standards and what Vite needs. That's where [`universal-middleware`](https://github.com/magne4000/universal-middleware) steps in: it's a minimal library built around web standards to fill the gap between web standards and common needs.

FYI, in the context of building [Vike](https://vike.dev), we tried to only use web standards but unfortunately realized that web standards alone aren't enough. That's why we built `universal-middleware`: it's the missing library that is unopinionated while filling the gap.

> [@jamesopstad](https://github.com/jamesopstad) thanks for the work on this workaround! Are there any drawbacks of using this approach since you're bypassing a fix that was made for something else?

The drawback is that it's possible to end up with multiple references for the same module. We try to discover the user's dependencies up front but in some cases dependencies are missed by Vite's dependency scanner. The scenario where this is problematic is if a new dependency is discovered late, during request handling. This may affect the pre-bundling of existing dependencies that have already been loaded and executed. In most cases this shouldn't cause issues but it's possible, for example, that there is some state stored in the module scope that leads to a mismatch.

For the time being, I think this is the right tradeoff as the `Error: There is a new version of the pre-bundle for ...` error is very frustrating and there's not currently a straightforward alternative to resolve it. It's also worth noting that the drawback outlined above was already present in Vite versions prior to 7.1.3 so we are effectively restoring that behaviour. The longer term fix is to use full-bundle mode rather than `optimizeDeps` in the Cloudflare plugin once that is supported in Vite for server environments.

The new Vite option is applied by default in v1.20.0 of `@cloudflare/vite-plugin` so if you upgrade `@cloudflare/vite-plugin`, `wrangler` and `vite` to the latest versions the issue should be resolved.

Can you explain why you're using .cts in a vite app?

We maintain [vivliostyle-cli](https://github.com/vivliostyle/vivliostyle-cli), a Node.js CLI application that loads JavaScript configuration files. We are currently working on adding TypeScript configuration file support (`.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`) using Node.js 22+ `--experimental-strip-types` flag (similar to how Prettier works).

The issue arises in [our test environment](https://github.com/vivliostyle/vivliostyle-cli/blob/40b4cdecfd409207bd6e4271d839296e681eea69/tests/config-typescript.test.ts#L57-L67). We use Vitest to test the config loading functionality, and when Vitest (running in SSR mode) tries to dynamically import a `.cts` file, Vite doesn't transpile it.

So to clarify: we're not using `.cts` in a Vite app itself—we're testing a Node.js CLI's `.cts` config support using Vitest, and the test fails due to this transpilation gap. In production, the CLI runs directly on Node.js, so `.cts` files work correctly.

The actual problematic line is [here](https://github.com/vivliostyle/vivliostyle-cli/blob/40b4cdecfd409207bd6e4271d839296e681eea69/src/config/load.ts#L62). When this dynamic `import()` is executed in Vitest (Vite's SSR mode), it goes through Vite's module resolution. Since Vite's esbuildPlugin filter regex doesn't include `.cts`, the file is passed directly to Rollup without being transpiled, causing a parse error. Also note that `.cjs` files work correctly since they are plain JavaScript and don't require transpilation. The issue is specific to `.cts` files which contain TypeScript syntax.
