However, when I tried to switch from a `single build` to `continuous watch`, I found that it was impossible to obtain `RollupOutput` no matter what I did.

After I continued to dive deeper into debugging the Rollup code, I discovered that this issue might not be resolvable only through Vite. This is because, in watch mode, Rollup does not pass any RollupOutput to any of its watcher events.

----
the key code is here:
https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/watch/watch.ts#L213

First, `.result` provided in the `BUNDLE_END` event is indeed the result from rollup; it implements the `RollupBuild` interface.

Then `RollupBuild` interface provides two functions, [**`generate()`**](https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/rollup/rollup.ts#L119) and [**`write()`**](https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/rollup/rollup.ts#L127), to produce a `RollupOutput`. These two functions are essentially the same, except for the first parameter `isWrite` being different when they call [`handleGenerateWrite()`](https://github.com/rollup/rollup/blob/b12c061d27d63062b91c1830a698de53fd6c2067/src/rollup/rollup.ts#L190).

When `skipWrite` is not true, the code uses an await call to `result.write()` to generate and write the code to files. It's precisely here that they, surprisingly, do not pass the `RollupOutput` generated by `result.write()` to the `BUNDLE_END` event.

When `skipWrite` is true, neither `generate()` nor `write()` are called, making it even more impossible for a RollupOutput to exist.

----
It's evident that this piece of code, including the `skipWrite` config, fails to cover the scenario of "generating without writing".

If it were up to me, I would change `skipWrite` to a configuration option more like `afterRollup: 'write' | 'generate' | false`.

Furthermore, I would save the result of either `result.generate()` or `result.write()` and include it in the `BUNDLE_END` event.

## Case Study

Here is a related problem that I just dealt with. For context, I need my app to be polyfilled for Chrome 49 and Safari 13.1.

Initially, I did not set `modernTarget`, but did set `target` and `build.target` to their respective equivalent syntaxes of Chrome 49 and Safari 13.1
- I got a polyfilled legacy bundle that worked as expected for Chrome 49, but Safari 13.1 was loading the modern bundle, and it was not polyfilled.
- Got warnings that `build.target` was being overridden by `modernTarget`, even though I didn't set it.
- There were legacy and modern bundles, but only legacy polyfills

It took me a minute to realize that if modern bundles are enabled (they are by default), then the boundary between the modern and legacy bundles is _Native ESM + native ESM dynamic import + import.meta_, no matter what the targets are set to. I also realized that the value of `modernTarget` is _always_ applied to my app, including if it still has the default value, and regardless of the value `build.target`.

By default, `modernPolyfills` is false. In order to polyfill Safari 13.1, I need to polyfill my modern bundle by giving `modernPolyfills` an appropriate value. The legacy bundle will never load in Safari 13.1 if `renderModernChunks` is true, because Safari 12 is the earliest Safari to support native ESM, native ESM dynamic import, and import.meta. If I set `modernPolyfills` to `true` ([not recommended](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#modernpolyfills)), then Babel will use all the [default(?)] `modernTarget` browsers, compared to what features are detected in my code (plugin-legacy [uses `useBuiltIns: 'usage'`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/ad5b3bf6f3ad7b24886718c5f5de32eee923ae11/packages/plugin-legacy/src/index.ts#L595)), to get a bunch of polyfills that cover every edge case. I think _most_ of the modern polyfills are redundant, which, I imagine, is why the devs recommend not doing that. For me, that was 58 polyfills for modern, compared to 81 polyfills for legacy. The easy way to see which polyfills are used is by running `DEBUG=vite:legacy pnpm build` with `modernPolyfills: true`.

For now, I still need to decide if I want to 
- just leave in the extra polyfills. Most of them are not cutting edge features, and babel is using `useBuiltIns: 'usage'`, so _something_ in that default browser list wants these polyfills _for my code_
- check each polyfill in the modern bundle against caniuse, and manually include the appropriate polyfills (assuming it's detecting some edge cases that I will likely never see - e.g. `Symbol: description` in iOS 12.1).
- use cloudflare's polyfill service
- do a single legacy build for all browsers
- modify my code to not use the features that require polyfills

So there are definitely some fuzzy bits where the config experience could be improved, and/or the docs could be fleshed out a bit. @nulladdict -I bumped into annoying target syntax too, and also found the unsetting of build.target to feel backwards.

> The ideal solution is for oxc, rolldown and then vite to support functionality that plugin-env provides. This way users can use oxc-based polyfill detection and entirely avoid plugin-legacy for modern build

Love this. Hopefully we get here. If we are very lucky, this will also work for legacy workers.

But, for now, I think my experience with this has some answers to @nulladdict 's lingering questions that might also be useful for others or for adding to the docs. Depending on what nulladdict finds in their investigation, I could do a PR to update docs later.


## Missing Answers

> if I don't set the option would build.target still be replaced by some default?

Yes. `build.target` is always replaced by `modernTarget` when using plugin-legacy, which currently has the default setting of `'edge>=79, firefox>=67, chrome>=64, safari>=12, chromeAndroid>=64, iOS>=12'`. If you set `modernTarget` to something else, `build.target` will be replaced by that. 

Additionally, I _think_ `build.cssTarget` will also inherit those values for the modern bundle. For sure, it will always be set to `'chrome61'` for the legacy bundle.

> won't build.target fallback to its default value?

No. The plugin [manually overrides build.target](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/ad5b3bf6f3ad7b24886718c5f5de32eee923ae11/packages/plugin-legacy/src/index.ts#L240C9-L248C10) after the config is loaded (`configResolved` hook(s)), but before each build/bundle (`generateBundle` hook(s)).

UNLESS you are wondering if it will fallback to its default before another plugin runs after plugin legacy? In that case.. maybe? I'm not sure about that. But subsequent plugins will be running after the code is built and bundled, so I don't imagine many cases where that will matter, right? I don't really know.

> if I want to both render legacy chunks and add modern polyfills what do I do?

Populate [modernPolyfills](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#modernpolyfills) with core-js 3 specifiers, and/or [additionalModernPolyfills](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#additionalmodernpolyfills) with paths to manually installed polyfills, or set to `true`.

Usually, you should not change the default `modernTargets` if you also want a legacy bundle. If you change any browsers in this list to a lower version than what they are now, nothing will change, because any lower version will load the legacy bundle anyway (`nomodule` etc). If you change it to anything higher, then there will be a gap of supported versions between the legacy bundle and whatever higher version you specify. That might be ok in your case, but would generally be undesireable.

e.g. 
- your code uses [Array.flatMap](https://caniuse.com/array-flat) (Chrome 69+)
- default `modernTarget` is >=Chrome 64
- you change `modernTarget` to >=Chrome 107 (vite's new default `build.target`)

The bit of built code that uses flatMap works in browsers <=Chrome63, and >=Chrome69 (where `flatMap` was introduced), but not any browser in between (i.e. Chrome 64-68).

I suppose if we wanted the modernTargets threshold to change, we would have to write a different detector. [Currently it is](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/ad5b3bf6f3ad7b24886718c5f5de32eee923ae11/packages/plugin-legacy/src/snippets.ts#L10C1-L10C125) 

```js
export const detectModernBrowserDetector: string = `import.meta.url;import("_").catch(()=>1);(async function*(){})().next()`

```

I think I can answer those questions. I think your questions are partly answered in the [vite build docs](https://vite.dev/guide/build). Plugin-legacy docs assume you are familiar with that already 

> 1. Suppose we're using a newer target such as baseline-widely-available or baseline 2021 or something similar. Does that mean that we do not need to use polyfills (either using a 3rd party or using @vitejs/plugin-legacy) at all?

Correct (mostly). You won't need `plugin-legacy` to cover browsers that vite can target natively (https://vite.dev/guide/build#browser-compatibility), which is to say, any browser target that esbuild can cover by transforming your codebase using syntax lowering without polyfills. So at some point, it depends a bit on what javascript features you are using in your code. But vite/esbuild _should_ throw an error at build time if there is a javascript feature in your codebase that can't be transformed for your target ([esbuild target docs](https://esbuild.github.io/api/#target)). If that happens, then you either need to get rid of it, or polyfill it. Plugin-legacy is just 1 option for polyfilling (but it's definitely the easiest).

> 2. And suppose we're using an older target, so old that those browser do not support native ESM. I think we need to use @vitejs/plugin-legacy here? For browsers that do support native ESM, the polyfills won't be loaded right? Does that mean those browsers do not need the polyfills? (which is question 1 again)

`plugin-legacy` makes 2 bundles by default, the threshold is `Native ESM + native ESM dynamic import + import.meta`, which translates to `edge>=79, firefox>=67, chrome>=64, safari>=12, chromeAndroid>=64, iOS>=12`. Any browser below these will load the legacy bundle, which is automatically polyfilled based on your target. If you need polyfills in the modern target, then you can manually set those with the `modernPolyfills` option, as described [in the docs](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/tree/main/packages/plugin-legacy#modernpolyfills).

Since esbuild throws an error if it can't transform something, before you even attempt to use plugin-legacy, I would set your target in the regular vite build options, and try building your app. If you get no errors, then you should be good to go! Obviously, you should still test in your target browsers to be sure.

> **Root Cause:**

The issue is in the parsing regex in packages/vite/src/node/plugins/workerImportMetaUrl.ts (line 212).
When Prettier formats new URL(..., import.meta.url) across multiple lines, it adds a trailing comma after import.meta.url:
Prettier formats long paths like this:

```
  const worker = new Worker(
    new URL(
      "../some-loooooooooooooooooong-file-path.js",
      import.meta.url,   // ← trailing comma
    ),
    { type: "module" },
  )
```

The Worker plugin's regex expects:
`  import.meta.url )`

  But Prettier produces:
`  import.meta.url, )`



> **Comparison with Asset Plugin**

Interestingly, the asset plugin (assetImportMetaUrl.ts) already handles this correctly:
Asset plugin regex (line 63-64) - WORKS ✅

```
  \bnew\s+URL\s*\(\s*('[^']+'|"[^"]+"|`[^`]+`)\s*,\s*import\.meta\.url\s*(?:,\s*)?\)/dg
                                                                          ^^^^^^^^^^
                                                             handles optional trailing comma
```

Worker plugin regex (line 211-212) - BROKEN ❌
```
\bnew\s+(?:Worker|SharedWorker)\s*\(\s*(new\s+URL\s*\(\s*('[^']+'|"[^"]+"|`[^`]+`)\s*,\s*import\.meta\.url\s*\))/dg
                                                                                   missing (?:,\s*)?  ^^^

```



> **Try**

Add (?:,\s*)? before the closing ) in the Worker parsing regex to handle optional trailing comma:

` - /\bnew\s+(?:Worker|SharedWorker)\s*\(\s*(new\s+URL\s*\(\s*('[^']+'|"[^"]+"|`[^`]+`)\s*,\s*import\.meta\.url\s*\))/dg`

to

`+ /\bnew\s+(?:Worker|SharedWorker)\s*\(\s*(new\s+URL\s*\(\s*('[^']+'|"[^"]+"|`[^`]+`)\s*,\s*import\.meta\.url\s*(?:,\s*)?\))/dg`



> **Verification**

 Test results:
1. Multiline with trailing comma:
    OLD regex matches: false  ❌
    FIXED regex matches: true ✅
2. Single line (no trailing comma):
    OLD regex matches: true   ✅
    FIXED regex matches: true ✅

The fix ensures both formats work correctly while maintaining backward compatibility.

Also this is similar to the recent fix in commit `130e7181a` which added multiline support for `import.meta.resolve` detection

I wouldn't handle them in prod! 😅 At least for the approach I've taken with CSP, there are two distinct plugins which implement CSP differently—an `apply: 'serve'` plugin which uses nonces (useful in dev), and an `apply: 'build'` plugin which computes JS hashes (useful to minimize transformation in production server), injects `integrity` attributes to `<script>` tags, and emits a full set of hashes to a separate file (to be consumed by the production server). This separation seems to make sense because during `vite dev`, Vite is doing the serving, but in `vite build`, the serving is done by the production server (e.g., Express, GitHub Pages, etc.), so there is a natural asymmetry around which entity is responsible for emitting HTTP response headers in either case.

But if one is forced to use use nonces in production, I believe the plugin must emit a placeholder during build in `transformIndexHtml` (e.g., `<script nonce="__NONCE_PLACEHOLDER__">`)—which requires only the `html` parameter; no other context required. When the Vite build output is served to customers, the HTML files must be transformed at serve time to inject the nonce generated by the server.

Thanks for clarifying your present feeling on the matter! I believe I may have run into one such caveat with `transformIndexHtml` in my implementation of the `apply: 'build'` plugin which computes hashes... As it turned out, `transformIndexHtml` runs _before_ some final JS transformations during build—namely `postImportMapHook()`:

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/055d2b86b0543a7c1a2a4d5bc7298af62bc51fa7/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/html.ts#L288-L293

As a result, if the JS chunk referenced from HTML were to be hashed in `transformIndexHtml`, its content would be different from the final output, and therefore the hashes wouldn't match. To work around this, the plugin uses a `generateBundle` hook with `order: 'post'` to defer hashing JS chunks until _after_ `postImportMapHook()` runs.

Zooming out a bit, the original thought behind exposing `req` and `res` within `transformIndexHtml` was not to upset the balance between build and serve modes, but rather to attempt to improve the ergonomics of working with the _current request/response_ during `vite dev/preview` only, without having any effect on `vite build`. By contrast, during build, Vite already runs the rich set of Rollup hooks, so the ergonomics of working with the current module/chunk/bundle already seem quite flexible and extensible by comparison (e.g., given the `generateBundle` example above).

For posterity: the solution to ordering issue is to change architecture of your css modules to never overwrite css properties declared on the base class. You should only build upon base class with new/unique properties but never overwrite. For complex cases you will have a tree of classes where only leaf nodes are actually used as classNames for HTML elements (you will also have plenty of mixins). Of course this only applies if you compose from other files - in the context of one file you can do whatever you want.

It feels to me that this is just a trait of CSS Modules in their current form and can not be fixed. To depend on ordering of CSS declarations feels fragile and prone to being mishandled by post processing plugins.

The problem here is that when a CSS Module is imported and it has a `composes`, Vite outputs all CSS to a single style element. This is the bug. Vite should output multiple style elements, one for each module. And, if a module of the same name has already been injected then simply do not output it again. After this there would be no more duplication of selectors. (Of course I'm no expert in Vite internals, behavior, nor limitations.)

I would like to see this fixed since I'm moving to Storybook 7 with Vite. This issue breaks our current code architecture. Many of our CSS Modules have zero specificity selectors in order to have no issues on consumer side of component library, avoiding potential issues with CSS file loading order. The existence of this bug forces me to increase specificity selectively based on whether a CSS Module uses `composes` or not. This will also force me to release a new major version of the library as increasing specificity is a potential breaking change. Also, working around this Vite `composes` issue will be extra mental load that nobody should be dealing with.

I think one of the reasons this issue does not come up that often is that you will mostly notice this issue if you are a veteran CSS Module user, or if you're moving existing code to use Vite. If you are less experienced with CSS Modules and/or are working on new code then you probably think CSS Modules is limited, and continue on.

The reason why this is happening is explained in #7651:

> ## Current Vite's implementation
> It is implemented by [this `rebaseUrls` function](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/09c4fc01a83b84f77b7292abcfe7500f0e948db6/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/css.ts#L1303-L1365). This function is called [inside `importer` option](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/09c4fc01a83b84f77b7292abcfe7500f0e948db6/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/css.ts#L1226) which is passed to sass. But importer will only be called if it is not a relative import because of the resolve order.
> 
> > Loads are resolved by trying, in order:
> > 
> > * Loading a file from disk relative to the file in which the @use or @import appeared.
> > * Each custom importer.
> > * Loading a file relative to the current working directory.
> > * Each load path in includePaths.
> > * Each load path specified in the SASS_PATH environment variable, which should be semicolon-separated on Windows and colon-separated elsewhere.
> > 
> > [Interface LegacyStringOptions importer](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/js-api/interfaces/LegacyStringOptions#importer)
> 
> Which means if a file is resolved by relative path, `rebaseUrls` functions won't be called. The example is below.
> 
> ```css-scss
> /* src/foo.scss */
> @import "./nested/bar.scss";
> /* @import "/@/nested/bar.scss"; */ /* if a alias is used `rebaseUrls` will be called */
> 
> /* ---- */
> /* src/nested/bar.scss */
> .bar {
>   background: url('./bar.png');
> }
> ```

_Putting my 2c on the issue._ 

### What's slowing it down

Through some profiling, we found that the amount of requests isn't an exact indicator of the slowness. You can have a JS file that imports 10000 raw JS files and it will be as fast too.

The slowness is caused by the need to transform the file, e.g. `.ts` -> `.js` and `.vue` -> `.js`. And this causes an internal waterfall where imports of files take turn to transform sequentially. So while we keep our internal Vite plugins fast, third-party plugins can also attribute to the performance impact, and they are out of our control.

### What can we do today

One way we can address this is by warming up some files so that they are transformed early and ready to go when requested: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/14291. [Here's also an in-depth explanation of why this approach](https://github.com/bluwy/vite-plugin-warmup?tab=readme-ov-file#why). The feature however doesn't cover warming up after HMR, but definitely doable soon.

### What about treeshaking

It's great that https://github.com/Dschungelabenteuer/vite-plugin-entry-shaking works too, but one of the main things I'm wary of is side-effects, as some files from the barrel export may rely on it work. Analyzing it is more expensive than warming up. But admittedly, most barrel files don't really export side-effects, so this shouldn't always apply, but it's still something we need to make correct if it were to be a core feature. (Also, not to mention risks of duplicated references of singletons with this approach.)

### Conclusion

So IMO, I think we should see how https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/14291 works, and only go with what this issue proposed as a last resort. If you'd like to debug slow plugins today, you can do so by running `DEBUG="vite:plugin-*" vite dev`, but take the logs with a grain of salt as measuring async code isn't reliable, but should still surface the more intensive work done.

Looks like this is indeed intentional. If you have:

```less
src: url('@{icon-font-path}/OpenSans-Regular.ttf?l4m091')
```

Vite doesn't know what the value of `icon-font-path` is ahead of time to correctly rebase it. It could be `https://some-cdn.com` for example, and that shouldn't be rebased. So any URLs that starts with a variable essentially tells Vite that "you're controlling how this path loads".

If you know this is a relative path, you can do something like this:

```less
src: url('./@{icon-font-path}/OpenSans-Regular.ttf?l4m091')
```

(adjust the value of `icon-font-path` accordingly). Now Vite knows that this is relative and it can rebase it. That does look like that's been a good prototyping path in the past!

For what it's worth, as a library author I have two main concerns:

- There is no single interoperable way to publish web worker instantiation code that works with all bundlers out of the box. `new URL(…, import.meta.url)` got close, but not quite.
- I can put a lot of work into using standardized vanilla JS workarounds, but people will still ask me what went wrong if my workarounds [cause other interoperability issues](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/14499).

Now that `import.meta.resolve(…)` is the interoperable solution supported by all browsers and runtimes, it would save me *lot* of headaches for it to work out of the box in a few major bundlers (particularly Vite). So if there's something that makes it as easy as possible to land in the core initially (e.g. leaving out `baseURL` support initially), this would help wrap up over a decade of pain for library authors like me.

I'd also be happy help author a plugin or a PR if it helps, but unfortunately I wouldn't be able to commit any time to ongoing maintenance.

Not to mention that, in reality, it may never end up making it in to the core if it's introduced as a plugin now. It would save a lot of headache down the road if it was included in core from the get-go.

Similar to #19042, it seems sass passes `#styles/base` as `file:///path/to/src/App.scss#styles/base` to Vite. `./src/App.scss#styles/base` is the same meaning with `./src/App.scss` in Vite. This is a limitation of sass's modern API and unfortunately I think there isn't a easy way to solve this.

Sass should never see any URLs with `#` in them, because in URLs `#` is a fragment identifier with special semantics and not just a generic separator. You should choose a different character to use for this before putting it in a Sass file or passing it to a Sass API.

Also, generally, anything that's a relative URL (that is, that doesn't begin with a scheme of the form `<alphanumeric>:`) will first be resolved relative to the file it contains. If you _don't_ want relative resolution behavior, we recommend you use a URL scheme like `vue:styles/base`.
Closing as a won't-fix since this is a limitation of sass's modern API.

We also ran into this issue at my company.

## Context

Prior to using vite, we used another build server via http with a url like `http://localhost:9002`. There are still a lot of legacy occurrences of this URL throughout our company: links generated in CI, browser history and bookmarks, etc. One of the main issues that keeps cropping up is that devs will enter the bare `localhost` into their address bar and it will autocomplete to the http version.

We want to continue using the same port so there isn't really an option to run a small side-car server to redirect.

## Our workaround

We are considering implementing the same approach as described above: a small tcp proxy that redirects http → https, and delegates https → the vite server. This works, but then we have to explain to devs to avoid calling `vite dev` which is a bummer.

This sounds like you need to fix your deployment strategy. I wonder why `vite optimize` works in your case.

The reload happens when a dependency was not found by crawling the static imports. But the `vite optimize` command also crawls the static imports in the same way. So there shouldn't be any dependencies that are only found by `vite optimize`.

One potential reason is that the crawl entry is not set correctly by Cypress. In that case, setting [`optimizeDeps.entries`](https://vite.dev/config/dep-optimization-options.html#optimizedeps-entries) for Cypress runs might help.

But even with that, `vite optimize` won't work if you have a dependency only imported from a dynamic imported module. To support that case, we'll need a more advanced command than `vite optimize` that crawls the whole graph instead of only the static imports.

Scan time Bundle time
optimizeDeps.include 256ms 6000ms

So it turns out it's not a Vite issue but a circular reference outside Vite using symlinks. It is very very common for begginers to do 

```bash
ln -s destination source
```

and then they think "oh well it doesn't work let's do the other one"

```bash
ln -s source destination
```

And this creates a full circle, resulting in a circular symlink.

If you do a `ln` and you think to yourself "it doesn't work" just make sure to `unlink` before doing a the other way around. Hope it helped, not really an issue with Vite

nuxt currently aliases `assets/*` to your assets directory here:
https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/blob/b0b1bb6fc18237c9ac2cdcd72a1261643584fbc1/packages/schema/src/config/common.ts#L512

without nuxt, things work, so this change would actually just be an optimisation (avoiding visiting the resolver by directly loading relative files).

however, this points out that relative URLs are currently eaten up by the resolve plugin.

if we load `assets/foo.js` from `/node_modules/package/index.js`, we clearly mean to load `/node_modules/package/assets/foo.js`, but the alias plugin will currently apply and override this.

so you could argue that the alias plugin should ignore `node_modules` paths.

but then what is the expected behaviour in other directories? if i load `assets/foo.js` from `/src/components`, what is the intent? `URL` behaviour suggests we should be loading `/src/components/assets/foo.js`, but `import` behaviour suggests we should use the alias plugin and load `/assets/foo.js`.

i feel like someone in the wild must be relying on being able to use these aliases in `URL` though. so maybe the best we can do is ignore `node_modules`

After some more investigation, it seems that the `info_hash` parameter is causing the malformed URL. The spec describes the `info_hash` as a "urlencoded 20-byte SHA1 hash".

As `decodeURI` expects all encoded parts prefixed with a `%` to be a valid UTF-8 character ([source](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/decodeURI#exceptions)) and not any byte, it causes the error.

One way to fix this would to implement a custom `decodeURI` function to handle other bytes. Currently, `decodeURI('%00')` returns `\u0000`, maybe something similar could be implemented so other bytes are converted. Or maybe just ignore those characters and leave as is.

Knowing these modes exist, is the `bundled` mode really meant to stay?

If I understand correctly, the `runner` mode should work in all cases. Externally, as a black box, it should be the same to the consumer of Vite (minus some quirks like the one described in this issue), while internally the process is different since it transpiles file by file instead of bundling. But it could really replace the `bundled` mode.

Now, the `native` mode is really great since it removes all the overhead and keeps the behavior of the runtime pristine, but I understand it can’t be set to replace the other modes since it implies a change on the user side: it requires a TypeScript compatible runtime. Though future improvement could do runtime detection to enable it by default.

Btw I just tried both `bun vite --configLoader runner` and `bun --bun vite --configLoader native`, and they work perfectly fine and fix my issue here. Ideally `bun vite` would use `runner` by default, and `bun --bun vite` would use `native` by default.

You can see in this test run: https://github.com/mainmatter/ember-vite-codemod/actions/runs/18342647216/job/52241625208#step:6:175 we have the issue, that is because we're building a Vite app into a temp directory and that is in a really long path in windows by default. 

In the linked stack trace you can see the path of the index-file has a long path: `C:/Users/runneradmin/AppData/Local/Temp/tmp-6140-eC0cWmnKQhgw/test-app/index.html?html-proxy&index=0.js` and you can also see in the stack trace that the long path truncating has kicked in: `file:///C:/Users/RUNNER%7E1/AppData/Local/Temp/tmp-6140-eC0cWmnKQhgw/test-app/node_modules/.pnpm/vite@6.3.6_@types+node@24.7.0_terser@5.44.0/node_modules/vite/dist/node/chunks/dep-Bu492Fnd.js`

Our solution for CI was to just define temp to be in `D:\Temp` on windows and it never hit the long-path truncation https://github.com/mainmatter/ember-vite-codemod/pull/67/files#diff-b803fcb7f17ed9235f1e5cb1fcd2f5d3b2838429d4368ae4c57ce4436577f03fR98-R102

This seems to be because CSS in Vite are side-effectful by default, so Rollup would proceed to render the chunk even if it's unused. We can't change that though since it would break many other tooling, though Vite supports the [`?inline`](https://vitejs.dev/guide/features.html#css) query to disable side effects, and you have to inject it manually.

I also found another bug, which after using `?inline`, the assets are still emitted, so that seems like a bug.

Update: I took another look at the issue today. The `index.css` (or `main.css` in the repro) is not included in the bundled CSS anymore, but the font assets are still emitted. It's because even though the import is unused, we would still transform it and it'll unconditionally emit the assets when transforming.

I'm not sure if there's a way for Rollup to skip transforming imports in dead code, I assume it doesn't treeshake after finished transforming/parsing a module. (Only during rendering?). So there isn't an easy fix on our side at the meantime, other that manually analyzing all assets emitted against the rendered chunks and delete them.

About the `?inline` issue, I found that it's the same cause as above.

If you are using NPM, then configure NPM to not auto-install optional peer dependencies.
Add `omit=optional` to your `.npmrc` file.
Then uninstall and reinstall Vite, which will first remove Vite and its dependencies from your package lock file, and then will only add Vite back with the _required_ dependencies. After that, manually install `sass` and don't install `sass-embedded`.

Sadly, NPM is a bit nuts and configuring optional dependencies to be omitted and then doing `npm un sass-embedded` when it's already installed, **won't work**. (Probably because the lock file still instructs that it's non-optional.)

Is it possible for a package to dynamically change it's dev dependencies based on the platform, or have platform-specific dependencies? I could not figure out how to use a package override to completely replace one package with another.

The existence of these two `sass` packages will create headaches for anyone developing on an unsupported platform unless every consumer checks that `sass-embedded` works. I can see everyone legitimately saying it's a different package's problem.

> Is it possible for a package to dynamically change it's dev dependencies based on the platform, or have platform-specific dependencies? I could not figure out how to use a package override to completely replace one package with another.

Yes. It's possible, but not dynamically in the sense of at the level of the dependent package.
Declaring the supported platforms is managed at the level of the dependency package itself.
Which means you also can't override anything about how the dependency is registered with the dependent, to make it vary by platform, where those instructions are absent or misconfigured.

See also https://github.com/npm/rfcs/discussions/120 which was meant to tackle this problem.
(Specifically by introducing `platformDependencies`.)

Development Mode (vite dev):
Vite serves files with native ES modules
The browser's native module system handles the imports
The browser's module loader sees broke:// as a valid URL protocol and tries to resolve it and throws cors error
Since broke isn't a registered protocol, it fails

Production Mode (vite preview):
Vite has already processed and bundled all imports during the build
All aliases are resolved to their final paths
The browser never sees the original broke:// protocol, 



The $ in $okay:// makes it an invalid protocol in URLs, which is why it gets passed through Vite's transform pipeline correctly in both dev and production.

i would recommend to use something that is not valid URL protocol like @ or ~ in prefix of the broke rather than $

Vite checks the internal lockfile that represents the current state of the `node_modules` (`./node_modules/.pnpm/lock.yaml` for pnpm). This is slightly different from the normal lockfile (`./pnpm.lock`). Even if Vite exposed the option, I'm not sure if Vite or the monorepo tool can have a proper document about this.
Instead of a normal option, Vite can add a special env var that is meant to be set by the monorepo tool. But I'm not sure if that's worth as I'm not aware of other tools moving the path of the lock files.
As an alternative, I think we can add
```js
{
  path: '.rush/temp/shrinkwrap-deps.json',
  // Included in lockfile
  checkPatchesDir: false,
  manager: 'pnpm',
},

I think it doesn't. If you mean `modulepreload`, it only applies to entry chunks and their direct imports. and `preload` is very different from `prefetch`,

where `preload` is
> specifying resources that your page will need very soon, which you want to start loading early in the page lifecycle, before browsers' main rendering machinery kicks in.

and `prefetch` is
> a hint to browsers that the user is likely to need the target resource for future navigations, and therefore the browser can likely improve the user experience by preemptively fetching and caching the resource.


Vite definitely won't `prefetch` the resources of potential future navigations by users. A use case can be lazying-loading routes, #5818 is a great example.

Both of the plugins mentioned above will not work well with large apps that does route level code splitting and it doesn't support Early Hints. On the other hand it's great for smaller apps, but if you want to go down the path of having a custom vite server and have fine grained control of what modules are used during the server render to preload the exact required modules as early as possible, you can use vite-preload.

Thanks for the quick response and the detailed explanation, bluwy. Your analysis makes perfect sense.

You're right that `dotenv` could be a solution in a custom script. However, the core issue arises when a user directly runs the `vite build --mode production` command. In this scenario, Bun pre-populates `process.env` from `.env.development` *before* the Vite CLI even starts executing. By the time Vite's internal `loadEnv` is called, it's too late – `process.env` already contains the wrong values, and Vite correctly prioritizes them. A user can't inject `dotenv` into Vite's internal build process to fix this.

This leads to a "silent failure" where the build succeeds but contains incorrect production variables, which can be very difficult to debug.

My goal with this issue was less about asking for a complex code fix and more about raising awareness. Given that Bun is gaining popularity as a runtime, other users will inevitably encounter this.

Perhaps the most practical solution would be to add a note to the Vite documentation? A small section on a "Common Issues" page or in the guide about using different runtimes, warning about Bun's default `.env` loading behavior and recommending the `bun --env-file=.env.production` or `NODE_ENV=production bun ...` workarounds would be immensely helpful for the community.
Yeah I think docs is probably the best way forward too. Maybe a short info block at https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode.html#env-files explaining the issue for Bun users.

Normally the dependency file only changes when the lock file changed or if it's a symlink to somewhere else. For symlink cases, Vite excludes the symlinks from the optimizer by default, so it isn't a problem.

In your case (npm `file:` + `--install-links`), the dependency files changes without the lockfile being changed even though it's not a symlink.
If removing `--install-links` works fine, I'd recommend that. If not, maybe using a package manager that updates the lock file when the content changes could solve your problem (I'm not sure if there're any though).

Webpack has a more complex approach for determining CSS Modules via `modules.auto`,
https://webpack.js.org/loaders/css-loader/#auto
Which supports:
```ts
type auto =
  | boolean
  | RegExp
  | ((
      resourcePath: string,
      resourceQuery: string,
      resourceFragment: string
    ) => boolean);
```

* `boolean` — enable/disable for all files
* `RegExp` — enable for files matching a pattern
* `function(resourcePath, resourceQuery, resourceFragment)` — custom logic per file

Not sure if I have enough context for this, but here's my understanding (for apps, no idea about libs).

Since vite outputs `<script type="module">` you can't get lower than `supports es6-module` without using the plugin-legacy.
Most real world apps would probably use dynamic imports, so the next tier is `supports es6-module and supports es6-module-dynamic-import`.

If you want to go more modern than the current default targets one place to start is browserslist's `defaults and supports es6-module and supports es6-module-dynamic-import`. You'll probably want to adjust the query according to your needs and your region. Also esbuild doesn't understand this syntax, but there's a plugin for that. More info here: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/11489

Now the most tricky part. There's a number of syntax features that esbuild cannot lower to a particular target environment. So if your app uses any of them you'll get a build error and you will probably have to raise your targets (or something might be not supported yet or at all). Some notable examples of features that require a higher targets are `import.meta`, `BigInt`, `top-level-await`, and `import-assertions`.

I don't know if there's an exhaustive list anywhere, but the code for downleveling js features lives here: [js_parser_lower.go](https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/blob/main/internal/js_parser/js_parser_lower.go) and required target versions can be found here: [js_table.go](https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/blob/main/internal/compat/js_table.go). Also I'm not sure if documenting esbuild internals is a useful thing for most of the users.

Edit: after reading a bit, it looks like new `using` syntax is already supported and one more unsupported feature is [`ArbitraryModuleNamespaceNames`](https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/pull/2154)

What if Vite used the `defaults` Browserslist query for consistency with other tools, but also pinned the dependency so the team can manage breaking changes to browser support manually? This should ideally be done in a major release to reduce impact of breaking changes.

## Rationale
 As @nulladdict mentioned in [playground for browsers that are in defaults, but don't have es modules or dynamic import](https://browsersl.ist/#q=defaults+and+not+supports+es6-module+and+not+supports+es6-module-dynamic-import), the difference in users is minimal (currently 1.1% globally and 0.18% in the US). Additionally, only Opera Mini and KaiOS users would be affected. Both of these browsers are primarily useful in markets with budget phones, which are more likely to not have touch or JavaScript support, and may require the legacy plugin for better support.

As far as I know esbuild doesn't support opera mini target, so browserslist-to-esbuild plugin just ignores it[^1].
As a result `defaults` currently translates to esbuild's `'chrome109', 'edge112', 'firefox102', 'ios15.6', 'safari15.6'`

I feel like it's a decent recommendation and covers everything that esbuild cannot downlevel. It updates automatically, so vite wouldn't need to keep track of changes unless we get some new compatibility issues with esbuild.

[^1]: https://github.com/marcofugaro/browserslist-to-esbuild/blob/main/src/index.js#L14

Spent some time on this recently and here's what i found.

* sourcemaps didn't work in vite1 too [1]
* simply returning the `map` from compileCss in vite:css [2] doesn't work [3] as it would need to be transformed to an actual SourceMap first [4]
* returning the correct sourcemap from vite:css alone does not help much, it needs to be passed on to the client too 

Figuring out how to pass on the sourcemaps is different for dev and build, both coming with their own set of challenges.
During dev, css is served from special js modules managing style nodes on the fly. So i think the easiest shot at this would be to add inline sourcemaps to that.

It seems a workaround is to use `target: new URL('/', 'http://localhost:3000')` instead of `target: new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')`.

I think this is an expected behavior change.

`http-proxy` does not receive `URL`, but receives the legacy [`url.Url`](https://nodejs.org/api/url.html#legacy-urlobject). `http-proxy-3` receives `URL` as well.
`new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')` is an instance of `URL` with some properties that overlaps with `url.Url`.
- For `http-proxy`, `new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')` was treated as `{ pathname: '/api', host: 'localhost:3000', ...otherProperties }` and `http-proxy` doesn't use the `pathname` property (it only reads the `path` property). So it was treated as `http://localhost:3000`.
- For `http-proxy-3`, `new URL('/api', 'http://localhost:3000')` is treated as an instance of `URL` and `http-proxy-3` uses the `pathname` property. So it is treated as `http://localhost:3000/api`.
This problem is due to the attribute decorator of https://github.com/Spencer17x/arca/blob/main/packages/awesome-babylonjs/babylonjs-mtoon-material/src/lib/mtoon-material.ts

In summary, if a library imports files from your project like this:

```
export async function loadView(path) {
    const views = import.meta.glob('/src/views/**/*.svelte');
    const module = await views[`/src/views/${path}.svelte`]();
    return module.default;
}
```

And you use it like this:

```
<script lang="ts">
    import { loadView } from 'mylib';
</script>
{#await loadView('foo')}
    Loading...
{:then Component}
    <svelte:component this={Component} />
{/await}
```

(and have `src/views/foo.svelte` with anything in it)

Then it caches `src/views/foo.svelte` aggressively using the same caching as `mylib` which leads to problems with things not updating properly or CSS not loading correctly.

This is less a library and more a "framework" - the framework is actually in control and calls down to the project rather than the other way around.

`maxParallelFileOps` limits the number of "load"s that can be processed concurrently. Setting it to 1 would disallow calling `this.load` inside the load hook because the load hook itself is already processing a "load" and `this.load` will cause another "load".
This is how `maxParallelFileOps` option in Rollup works (https://github.com/rollup/rollup/issues/5848) and Vite itself doesn't have control of it.

Vite treats all CSS files as side-effectful by default, that means even if we didn't used `B`, we still imported `B`, and `B` contains an import to a CSS file, that CSS file "effects" the state of the application (which makes sense because you add global styles), so that CSS is included in the final bundle, or else your application state could be inconsistent.

```diff
  "sideEffects": [
-    "*.css",
    "src/components/a/index.js",
    "src/components/b/index.js"
  ],
```

So in conclusion I think when there is `sideEffects` field, Vite should respect the field for css files (and others).

`ssrLoadModule` only works on ESM code. Since you've added `resolve.noExternal: true`, dependencies are also included in part of `ssrLoadModule` which won't work if the dependency is written in CJS. Usually this is handled by only setting `resolve.noExternal: true` during build only if it's needed to bundle the deps.

I gave this a go, but it looks like `resolve.noExternal: false` doesn't work well with the way Deno resolves modules. If set to `false` it seems like vite bypasses the plugin system entirely and assumes that it can use the node resolution algorithm for bare specifiers. This is not correct in the Deno world as there are no guarantees how the `node_modules` folder is laid out. It might be using the global cache dir or the local `node_modules` directory.

Disabling that option also breaks custom aliases in Deno for the same reason as bare specifiers are not passed through the plugin system anymore. JSR imports are also broken (again because they're not passed through the plugin system anymore).

The way resolution in Deno works is that it's important _where_ resolution is kicked of. It doesn't work like in node where it just bubbles up the directory tree to find a matching `node_modules/<pkg>` directory. It seems like this is assumed though internally in vite.

I'm eager to find a solution for this but I'm not sure what the intended path forward is that would fit well with vite internals. I'm stuck.

Issue:
Running `npm run dev` caused the following error:

TypeError: crypto.hash is not a function

Vite `v7.x` and above use the new `crypto.hash()` API, which is only available in:

Node.js v20.19.0+
Node.js v22.12.0+

Only works if your version of Node is v18.20.4, which does not support  this method.


✅ Solution:

1. Install NVM (Node Version Manager) if not installed:

   bash:
   curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash
   source ~/.zshrc


2. Installed supported Node version in your vscode terminal or mac terminal:

   bash:
   nvm install 22.16.0
   nvm use 22.16.0
   

3. Reinstalled dependencies:

   bash : 
   rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
   npm install
   

4. Ran dev server successfully:

   bash:
   npm run dev


Result:

In case it's helpful, here is the desired workflow:

1. Build docker image
2. Docker build container performs vite build
3. Docker build container copies static serving files to Nginx image to finish building production container
4. Production container is run in production environment with env variables set to their desired values
5. Production container initialization script writes those env variables to the proper env/json/whatever file before serving starts
6. App can use config values provided by the production container rather than the build container

Currently, step 2 causes production replacement to occur in the build container, meaning that the process can't change the env values from that point on. To use different env values for the container, you'd have to build the container again, meaning you'd need a different container image for every environment.
Currently there are some libraries to do that (e.g. https://iendeavor.github.io/import-meta-env/), but having this built-in would be great

> Do you know if there's any similar env var names?

A long long time ago, create-react-app used to check the `HOST` environment variable to determine which domains are valid. This was to support Cloud9(!) I'm not sure if we want something that generic as a name, though. Django has a setting called `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, but it does not support setting it as an env var as far as I know. Something more internal like `__VITE_DEV_ORIGIN` would also work.

> I wonder if there is a way for codesandbox to avoid the cross origin setup here or use existing means to configure the dev server eg hook the vite dev call and change it to vite dev --hostname xxxx --port yyyy

There is a way... if we manually let the proxy forward header `Host: localhost` when proxying a request instead of `Host: :id-5173.csb.app`. We used to do that initially, but it broke some other sandboxes. For example, Bun uses the `Host` header to determine its injected URLs when serving html (so the static assets would link to localhost, but they should instead link to `:id-3000.csb.app`).

One thing I could try... is to only forward `Host: localhost` if the port is 5173, but it would be an imperfect solution.

Overriding the binary is a bit more tricky, because when people fork a sandbox it is live cloned, so the running Vite process is cloned as well, it will continue running inside the child. But the hostname _did_ change, so then we'd have to restart Vite with the new `--hostname`.

So we could also transparently fix it on our side by changing the proxy, but the environment variable feels a bit cleaner. It depends on what you're most comfortable with in terms of implementation.

if there is a less hacky way for you to detect when to change the proxy and when not (what happens if someone were to use bun+vite?) i think i'd prefer that over adding a way to configure vite via environment variables. 

That could set a dangerous precedent and we have to answer a lot of questions like which value wins if both are set, what happens if the env value changes and the dev server is still running, will it pick up the new value when there is an automatic restart? Do we have to watch that value?
if you are able to add a `vite-plugin-codesandbox` you could also ensure the configuration with a config hook (and possibly read from env in that without requiring vite to do it internally).

I find the `VITE_` prefixing to be quite annoying. 

In my case, I wanted to show the git sha1/branch to easily tell what version is deployed.
By default this required re-exporting the CI environment variables.

```bash
export VITE_VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_REF=$VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_REF
export VITE_VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_SHA=$VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_SHA
```

Changing the prefix to `PUBLIC_` doesn't really help in this case. 
It's still a lot of error-prone copy/pasting.

Additionally, I would sometimes introduce a `import.meta.env.ABC` in a typescript file, but forget to update the build script. So it would silently fail.

My current solution is to centralize all client-only environment variables to one file.

`client-env-vars.ts`

```ts
export const VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_REF = process.env.VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_REF
export const VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_SHA = process.env.VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_SHA
```

Components have to go through this file to use environment variables.

`DebugPage.vue`

```ts
import { VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_REF, VERCEL_GITHUB_COMMIT_SHA } from '../client-env-vars'
```

Vite directly imports this file and replaces the `process.env.*` via `define`:

`vite.config.ts`

```ts
import * as envVars from './client-env-vars'

const define: Record<string, string | undefined> = {}
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(envVars)) {
  define[`process.env.${key}`] = JSON.stringify(value)
}

export default defineConfig({
  define
})
```

I don't know what the best solution is, but I think ideally:

- No need to prefix
- Declare environment variable names once
- Type-safe

Vite can not correctly deal with dependency chains of mixed ESM and CJS:

App -> ESM works
App -> CJS works
App -> ESM -> ESM works
App -> ESM -> CJS fails

There is a suggested workaround via [optimizeDeps.include](https://vitejs.dev/config/dep-optimization-options.html#optimizedeps-exclude) that each module consumer would have to add, so it's far from a usable solution.

The only reliable workaround is to bundle your ESM modules that have CJS dependencies themselves, but that comes at the cost of  dependency duplication.

### Summary of what was discussed in the above issue
The "[" in the path part is not allowed in [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986) (successor to [RFC 2396](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2396)), but is allowed in the URL Standard.

Both Node.js and browsers parses relative import specifiers in compliance with the [URL Standard](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/).

[^no]: https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#import-specifiers
[^bro]: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#resolve-a-module-specifier

So this is a valid JS in both browser and Node.js.

However, the Java server used rejects this URL because it is compliant with RFC3986, not the URL Standard.

Umm, rereading the URL Standard spec, it seems I'm wrong.
"[" (0x5B) in the path part is allowed in [the URL "representation" section](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-representation), but it's not allowed in [the "URL writing" section](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-writing).

Because `new URL('https://example.com/[foo]').href` returns `https://example.com/[foo]`, I thought "[" is allowed in the URL Standard spec. But it seems `.href` may return a invalid URL. I didn't expect that to happen. 🫠

> The output of the [URL serializer](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url-serializer) is not always a [valid URL string](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#valid-url-string).
> https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#urls:~:text=The%20output%20of%20the%20URL%20serializer%20is%20not%20always%20a%20valid%20URL%20string.

related: https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/379, https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/753

Any id that would be handled by a later plugin might be passed to the `resolveId` hook. So plugins should ignore errors whenever it makes sense to leave it for the later ones.
In this case, Vite's internal plugin is using [the virtual module convention](https://rollupjs.org/plugin-development/#conventions:~:text=If%20your%20plugin%20uses%20%27virtual%20modules%27%20(e.g.%20for%20helper%20functions)%2C%20prefix%20the%20module%20ID%20with%20%5C0.%20This%20prevents%20other%20plugins%20from%20trying%20to%20process%20it.), so it's expected to be handled by other plugin and the plugin should avoid throwing errors for them.

[Express 5 has added support](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html) for this:

>Request middleware and handlers that return rejected promises are now handled by forwarding the rejected value as an Error to the error handling middleware. This means that using async functions as middleware and handlers are easier than ever. When an error is thrown in an async function or a rejected promise is awaited inside an async function, those errors will be passed to the error handler as if calling next(err).

I just tested and polka has support for it as well. If there's an unhandled error in an `async` handler then `options.onError` will be called. - resolveId: if `raw` and/or `url` query parameters are present, strip them, this.resolve the resulting id and and prefix it with `\0(raw|url|rawurl):`

  - If it contained `url`, store the loaded data as an asset and generate the URL as before
  - if it contained `raw`, generate a JS file as before
- transform: the `\0` ensures that the load result doesn't get transformed further

I think there are possibly two separate issues being described by different users/teams in this thread:
1. failed to fetch after a new deployment where the old version was deleted from the server
  - in this case, attempting to load the resource referenced by the error is expected to fail, it has been deleted
2. failed to fetch that occurs somewhat randomly
  - in this case, attempting to load the resource succeeds

For people experiencing issue 1., the solution is to organise your deployments so that old versions aren't deleted immediately. Doing a deployment of new app code doesn't mean that all users running your app in their browser will update immediately (unless you force it somehow).

For those users who still have an older version running in their browser (lets say `index.123.js`), navigating to routes that load chunks dynamically will always reference the chunk that was current when they loaded your app (ie `home.123.js`), and this is correct. You don't want the user getting half of their chunks with new app code and half with old, this would lead to very hard to debug issues. If you delete those chunks while the user is still navigating around the app, you will hit this error when they change routes and try to load a chunk they haven't loaded yet.

For users that load the app after a deployment, `index.html` will reference a new `index.456.js` chunk that references all the other chunks that are consistent with that version (ie `home.456.js` if there are also changes in that chunk). The only difference is which version was referenced by `index.html` when the user loaded the tab.

If you keep a manifest of each deployment, and your instrumentation/logging includes the "version" of the app users are using, you should be able to figure out how long old versions are still used. My team has seen users still operating in the same tab they loaded a month ago without updating, so we keep all our built assets deployed for a long time. If you want to force users to reload when a new version is deployed, that's a whole piece of engineering in itself.

I agree that:
- The `<meta property="csp-nonce">` is for internal use, and that any use of CSP's nonce feature should be complemented by setting the appropriate HTTP header (`Content-Security-Policy` with the corresponding nonce value.)
- The `html.cspNonce` is meant to hold a placeholder that is replaced server-side.

Based on this, I think the core of my suggestion might be adapted to still provide a better docs experience:

My concern is that the typical reader will often have an SPA (maybe with some traditional-server deployment) use-case in mind.

Even if the user were to implement the `http.nonce` placeholder, and replace it programatically on each request, I think this workflow is at odds with the typical static-file hosting of SPA. So a reader might:
1. Incorrectly build with a "static nonce."
2. Implement it properly, but at the cost of HTTP caching.

@niksy
### How this happens is:

When the web socket connection was disconnected, Vite's HMR client starts to ping to `http://yourserver/websocket-path`.
https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/29abeeab9cc147c6d3383c672ded68311304bbaf/packages/vite/src/client/client.ts#L311-L333
When the Vite server starts, Vite will respond to that ping request.
Then, Vite's HMR client reload the page.
https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/29abeeab9cc147c6d3383c672ded68311304bbaf/packages/vite/src/client/client.ts#L103-L105

But this has some edge cases. For example, when WebSocket server starts after the HTTP Server (can happen in middleware mode).

### Where we need to change is:

- Change the ping to use WebSocket instead of HTTP: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/29abeeab9cc147c6d3383c672ded68311304bbaf/packages/vite/src/client/client.ts#L311
- Handle that WebSocket connection: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/29abeeab9cc147c6d3383c672ded68311304bbaf/packages/vite/src/node/server/ws.ts#L80

I guess we need to use a different [protocol](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket/WebSocket#protocols)(`sec-websocket-protocol`) to differentiate the normal connection and the ping connection.

When tailwind has `foo.html` in `content` option, it registers that as a dependency of `bar.css` (the content is `@tailwind base;` and others).

I thought of that. But there's nothing available to all hooks that you can use to maintain multiple states. If you used something like a weak map with the resolved config as key, then subsequent hooks would need to be passed the resolved config to do the lookup, and not all of them are. Same goes for any other potential key/reference option.

Also, you were addressing restarts (rebuilds?). You mentioned using the build start hook. This isn't that. For that, mutating the current state is acceptable, because (re)builds/starts are serial/non-parallel within a single command invocation, and therefore part of a single lifecycle (though a bit of an edge case, and just squeaking by). I'm talking about running two commands, in parallel, one as a side effect of the other.

Even if there turns out to be a way to handle all cases of plugin reuse that I haven't thought of, the methods for handling them would definitely be outside the expectations for plugin design. It's not something a plugin writer would reasonably be expected to handle. The plugin factory closure is expected (assumed) to be a de facto "pre-command-start" hook.

To simplify the scenario: if someone were to instantiate (configure) a plugin once, capturing the returned plugin instance, and then use the JavaScript API to pass it into two parallel build commands, and that caused the plugin to behave incorrectly, I would expect the plugin author to tell the user that they used the plugin incorrectly. The solution would be to please reconfigure (recall the plugin factory function) for each build invocation. But, in the scenario I'm positing, where a plugin wants to run a JavaScript API command that inherits config (plugins) from the parent command, there's no way to currently reinstantiate the inherited plugins.

Regarding multiple builds, with Environment API, we now have an answer to [sharing plugin state across builds](https://vite.dev/guide/api-environment-plugins.html#environment-in-build-hooks). We may explore making plugins shared by default during build, so sharing state across builds in the same process would be the default.

About starting the preview server, we now have the `buildApp` hook that gives you a better way to add code once all the environments are already built. `vite build` is intended to build your application only. I don't think we should add a way to get reuse the InlineConfig for an unrelated command like preview. Maybe you could kick start a new `vite preview` process that will read the config again. Let's close this issue for the moment, and if you have further ideas, please open a new one that builds on top of all the new APIs we added in Vite 6.

This is a problem with `cleanUrl`. In files, allow `?` and `#` as part of the file name, but in URLs, there may be too many variations. Simply replacing `#` and `?` may not meet all requirements.

Similarly, `import "./in#.css";` cannot be handled correctly.

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/db5fb48f5d4c1ee411e59c1e9b70d62fdb9d53d2/packages/vite/src/shared/utils.ts#L31-L34

> Similarly, `import "./in#.css";` cannot be handled correctly.

I took a look, when the file name contains a `#`, the browser does not send anything after the `#` to the server. For example, when accessing `/c#.svg`, the browser will only send `/c` to the server. So even if the matching issue with `cleanUrl` is fixed, there is still no way to find the corresponding file based on the URL transmitted by the browser.

We discussed this feature in a recent team meeting and we decided that the best path forward is:
- Vite will leave import maps definitions untouched.
- A new [`external` config option](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/6582) will be implemented, that allows to define that an id is external for both dev and build.
- Users will need to add all the entry ids from import maps to this new `external` config option.

Vite has a single module graph for its server. If you have two modules imported by different HTML entry points, they will be a single module node in graph. Vite could automatically read the import map and respect it without `external` but that will be a big change in the conceptual model of Vite dev. Every module should start having a `?entry=path.html` query for example. We are also able to request a module in isolation, but this will break. Having the entries of the import map as `external` avoids these issues.

I have created a plugin to solve this issue during development, until official support is implemented:

https://github.com/MilanKovacic/vite-plugin-externalize-dependencies

From my analysis:
- The issue occurs because `revokeObjectURL` is called in the `finally` block, invalidating the Blob URL before WebKit workers can use it.
- WebKit requires the Blob URL to remain valid for the worker's lifecycle.
- Based on @sapphi-red’s suggestion, moving the `revokeObjectURL` call **inside the worker script** should resolve this issue.

I will update [`vite/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/worker.ts`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/worker.ts) to:
1. Remove the `revokeObjectURL` call from the `finally` block.
2. Ensure it's called inside the worker script instead.
3. Test the fix in Playwright WebKit.

You only install them if you use any of it. The issue here is package managers fetching metadata from those packages even though they're optional, which I'm not sure why they do.

As for npm: https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-json#peerdependenciesmeta

> Npm will not automatically install optional peer dependencies

So npm will not install them, but I can't speak for other package managers. Imho it'd still be better for them to be removed and for users to be required to explicitely install them.

All package managers will not install optional peer dependencies by default. They are optional. The issue is that they're fetching metadata for them even if they're not installed.

> and for users to be required to explicitely install them.

That's already how it is today. I don't really understand the proposal here. We cannot just remove them from `package.json`, unless you want us to remove CSS preprocessors support entirely and break the entire ecosystem.

> The issue is that they're fetching metadata for them even if they're not installed.

Yeah, pnpm (and possibly others?) fetching metadata sounds like a bug in those package managers.

> We cannot just remove them from package.json, unless you want us to remove CSS preprocessors support entirely and break the entire ecosystem.

At which point does the optional peer dependency become relevant? The [docs](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#css-pre-processors) already specify the user has to `npm add` preprocessors. What does the peerDependency actually achieve in such a case?

It declares the additional dependencies that vite can import, and the versions that Vite supports. In a strict installation, packages can only import the declared deps and peer deps. You can't import some arbitrary dep, and if it somehow works, potentially getting the wrong version. An optional peer deps means additionally package managers don't have to install it and vite can function normally with it not installed, until the user manually installs it.

I'd suggest reading some resources/docs on how optional peer deps work.

But why does vite need to import them in first place? Wouldn't it be better if CSS preprocessors were plugins? Given that CSS preprocessors are mostly obsolete today, I'd appreciate them being moved to plugins.

I'm also in favor of moving them to separate plugins so the main package stays lean. Not sure how feasible it is but given the problems around peer dependencies, I'm not entirely sold on keeping them around. Though it makes sense that something similar like this happening is unlikely.

Ok so in summary we have two potential action points:

1. pnpm should not attempt to fetch metadata for packages it's not going to install (I'm not going to file a issue because I don't use pnpm)
2. vite to potentially extract the CSS preprocessors to plugins (in a future major version)

I don't really think moving them as plugins is going to help much. It causes more friction for users who want to use CSS preprocessors and isn't worth the effort to have everyone migrate again. This really seem like an edge case in package managers that should be fixed there. I'm happy to be proven wrong though but again, optional peer dependencies are normal patterns in libraries and I don't think there's a reason they should be avoided.

This looks like a bug since Node handles `@/pkg` as _packageName_ https://nodejs.org/docs/latest/api/esm.html#resolution-algorithm (it's mentioned as `If packageSpecifier does not start with "@" ... Otherwise, ...` in `PACKAGE_RESOLVE`).

I have no control over the reverse proxy. (I use a private cloud solution that allows me to create development VMs.)

When I request `/` from by browser, I get a VSCode web IDE to develop my Vue app.
When I request `/proxy/5050/` from by browser, I get the homepage of my Vue application.
(The proxy strips the `/proxy/5050/` part of the URL and calls the dev server with the following part of the URL.)

> ...probably setting base to / [only for dev](https://vite.dev/config/#conditional-config) would work...

Unfortunately not. The request for `/src/main.ts` would not hit the Vue dev server, but the VSCode server.

**To summarize:**

The problem is that the URLs of the resources requested by the client must contain the `/proxy/5050/` base to hit the Vue dev server.
(Problem solved by setting a `BASE_URL`.)

 But by setting a `BASE_URL`, the Vue dev server expects the calls to be prefixed with the `/proxy/5050/` url base, wich does not happen (the base URL being striped at the proxy level).

We need a way to tell the Vue dev server to keep adding a base URL to the resources URLs (`/proxy/5050/`), but to still serve the resources from `/` (this is more subtle than this - see the _Suggested solution_ section of my initial message.)

Vite will mistake the text `<header>` inside that title for a `<head>` tag.

I alleviated a similar issue a while back in [hugo](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/commit/9dc608084b73f04c146351cbe8d1b2f41058e8ba) and found the same problem in [VS Code](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-livepreview/issues/711#issuecomment-2807935577) a couple weeks ago. The problem is threefold:
-   Using regular expressions to naively **search** for tags within an arbitrary HTML fragment is impossible. Many constructs can be nested and hold arbitrary text that looks like tags, so determining if a piece of code is actually a tag is impossible without context.
-   Beyond that, using regular expressions in the form `/<tagname[^>]*>/` to match entire tags isn't reliable. This leads to injections after `<header>` instead of `<head>` or inside an attribute value that contains a `>`.
-   Scanning through the whole document for a specific injection point, then falling back to searching for another injection point, is inefficient and increases the risks of false positives.

I recommend scanning the document from the start, and only reading past whitespace, comments, the doctype, the html tag and the head tag. HTML comments cannot be nested so they can be consumed reliably, and the risk of encountering a breaking attribute on the `<html>` or `<head>` tags are low.

As you know, files that is not included in the `exports` field cannot be accessed via `import`. This is how Node.js works.

If package "a" accesses like that, package `a` is broken and it should be fixed on the package "a" side.
If package "b" added such an `exports` field in a minor or patch version, that is a error in that package. Because adding that is a breaking change.
If package "b" added it in a major version, then package "a" won't have a problem because package "a" would still be able to use the old version.

If you need to workaround it, you can patch the package "a"'s package.json to be:
```json
  "exports": {
    "./*.js": "./*.js"
  }
```
You can also make a plugin for it if that's preferred.

I don't think Vite should allow non-standard things.

Possible reason from my investigation:

Considering the code like this:
`new URL("test.wasm", import.meta.url)`

In dev mode, when a JavaScript file contains such code, the `asset-import-meta-url` plugin will rewrite the `"test.wasm"` part into an absolute path.
- This works for JavaScript files in the repo
  (eg. the code from a JavaScript file in /src/a/b/c/x.js will be rewritten as `new URL("/src/a/b/c/test.wasm", import.meta.url)`)
- This does not work for JavaScript files from packages
  (eg. the code from a JavaScript file in /node_modules/test-wasm-library/index.js will be rewritten as `new URL("/node_modules/.vite/deps/test.wasm", import.meta.url)`)

"/node_modules/.vite/deps/test.wasm" does not exist, so the page fails to load. The correct path should be "/node_modules/test-wasm-library/test.wasm"

While Vite can support `this.fs` (https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/20301), it is currently unclear whether the `fs` option can be supported.

In the future, [Vite will migrate to Rolldown](https://vite.dev/guide/rolldown.html), and Rolldown may not be able to support the `fs` option.

<details>
<summary>fs option support in Rolldown</summary>

File system calls in oxc_resolver (a dep used in Rolldown) are sync. To support the `fs` option, we would need to either make these calls async or work around it by using `tokio::block_in_place`. However, it's unclear whether this would work reliably and whether the perf degration would be acceptable.

</details>

Until we're confident that the `fs` option can be implemented in Rolldown, I think Vite should avoid supporting it.

It appears that Vite deliberately strips the import attribute syntax:

https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/3af02bde7e7f26889d5c0eb300219c43ed1293ad/packages/vite/src/node/plugins/importAnalysis.ts#L494-L497

Worth noting that import attributes are [supported by TypeScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-3.html#import-attributes) along with [native support in Chrome](https://caniuse.com/mdn-javascript_statements_import_import_attributes).

It would be great it `vite` could avoid adulterating the import syntax in my code so that the runtime itself can interpret what I authored.

The workaround right now:

```
// vite strips the type declaration syntax
import stylesheet from './demo-badge.css' with { type: 'css' };

// vite does not modify the syntax
const { default: stylesheet } = await import('./demo-badge.css', { with: { type: 'css' } });
```

Some prior comments on the topic:
* https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/12140#issuecomment-1440150314
* https://github.com/vitejs/vite/issues/10633#issuecomment-1534125299

As a first step toward solving this issue, I think it might be nice to have an option to disable the current CSS runtime behavior entirely.

In other words, `*.css` files would be treated the same as any non-JS file type (e.g. `*.mdx`, `.tsx`, etc.), and plugins would be able to transform the CSS files to JS as needed.

This would fit the usecase of the [LWC framework](https://lwc.dev/) – in LWC, importing a CSS file returns a function:

```js
import stylesheet from './styles.css' // imports a function that returns a string
```

Currently, this functionality doesn't work in Vite even with our Rollup plugin (`@lwc/rollup-plugin`), due to Vite's default handling of CSS. (I have [a minimal repro](https://github.com/nolanlawson/lwc-vitest-demo/tree/test-styles-rendered) of this issue using Vitest.)

Unfortunately, the `?inline` or `with { type: 'css' }` solutions would not work for us, because it would be a breaking change for existing components (which do not use such syntax when importing stylesheets).

Potentially, our Rollup plugin could apply these transformations itself (to the `.js` files that are importing `.css` files), but I wonder if a more generic "disable the current CSS behavior" option would be a simpler solution for other web component frameworks in general.

> The modern browser detection script containing `import.meta.url` throws a syntax error on Android 8.0, preventing the legacy fallback from loading and causing a white screen.

This description doesn't sound correct. The modern browser detection script contains `import.meta.url`, so that legacy browsers throw an error there. If an syntax error happens, the next script tag loads the legacy entry point.
```html
<!-- modern browser detection script -->
<script type="module">import.meta.url;import("_").catch(()=>1);(async function*(){})().next();if(location.protocol!="file:"){window.__vite_is_modern_browser=true}</script>
<!-- the next script tag -->
<script type="module">!function(){if(window.__vite_is_modern_browser)return;console.warn("vite: loading legacy chunks, syntax error above and the same error below should be ignored");var e=document.getElementById("vite-legacy-polyfill"),n=document.createElement("script");n.src=e.src,n.onload=function(){System.import(document.getElementById('vite-legacy-entry').getAttribute('data-src'))},document.body.appendChild(n)}();</script>
```

For the first point (`glob` is bundled):

Vite externalizes dependencies that are not possible to resolve from the application. In this case, `glob` is not a dependency of the application and does not exist in `node_modules/glob` and is externalized.
If you run `deno add -D npm:glob`, `glob` gets externalized.

It seems bun generates `node_modules/glob`, which is a [phantom dependency](https://rushjs.io/pages/advanced/phantom_deps/), a transitive dependency that are possible to resolve from the application. 

This is an expected behavior.

For the second point (`node:` prefix is lacking):

This is because `glob` has a import to `fs` without `node:`. Vite does not add or remove `node:` automatically.
